quiz.q:
Design the plug gauge set, twice, in two unit systems

Problem. A hole is specified 25.000 / 25.021 mm. Using a gauge-maker's tolerance of 10% of the work tolerance and a wear allowance of 5%, both disposed inside the work tolerance zone, give the limits of the GO and NO-GO plug gauges. State the band of hole sizes that is certain to be accepted whichever gauges the shop is issued, and what fraction of the work tolerance that is. Then repeat the design for a hole specified 1.0000 / 1.0008 in.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The work tolerance is \( T = 25.021-25.000 = 0.021\ \mathrm{mm} \), so \( t_g = 0.10T = 0.0021 \) mm and \( w = 0.05T = 0.00105 \) mm.

(2) The GO plug embodies MMC, the smallest hole, 25.000. Its wear allowance is placed into the hole's material side so the gauge starts oversize and wears toward the limit: low limit \( 25.000+0.00105 = 25.00105 \), high limit \( 25.00105+0.0021 = 25.00315 \). It is withdrawn from service when it wears back to 25.000.

(3) The NO-GO plug embodies LMC, the largest hole, 25.021, and takes no wear allowance because it does not enter parts. Its tolerance is disposed inward: 25.0189 to 25.0210.

(4) A hole is certainly accepted if it admits the largest GO plug and refuses the smallest NO-GO plug, so between 25.00315 and 25.0189: a band of \( 25.0189-25.00315 = 0.01575\ \mathrm{mm} = 15.75\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(5) \( 0.01575/0.021 = 0.75 \), so 75% of the work tolerance survives. The 25% lost is \( t_g + w \) at the GO end and \( t_g \) at the NO-GO end — \( 10+5+10 \) per cent.

(6) In inches: \( T = 0.0008 \) in, \( t_g = 0.00008 \), \( w = 0.00004 \). GO plug 1.00004 / 1.00012 in; NO-GO plug 1.00072 / 1.00080 in; guaranteed band \( 1.00072-1.00012 = 0.00060 \) in, again exactly 75%.

Answer: GO 25.00105 / 25.00315 mm, NO-GO 25.0189 / 25.0210 mm, guaranteed band 15.75 µm = 75% of \( T \); in inches GO 1.00004 / 1.00012, NO-GO 1.00072 / 1.00080, band 0.00060 in = 75%. Sanity check: the 75% is a property of the two percentages, not of the size or the unit — which is why the inch design lands on the same fraction. Note the direction of every disposition: each gauge limit was moved so that a gauge at the worst end of its own tolerance still cannot accept a bad hole. Reverse either one and the guarantee inverts — the gauge set would then be capable of passing a hole outside its limits, which is the one thing a limit gauge exists to prevent.

quiz.q:
The bore that measures perfectly and will not assemble

Problem. A bore for the \( \varnothing25\,\mathrm{H7/g6} \) fit measures 25.010 mm at every section, but its axis is bowed 0.008 mm off straight. Find the largest straight cylinder that will pass through it. Give the verdict from a full-form GO plug gauge at 25.000 and from a two-point bore micrometer, and find the clearance left on a shaft at its own MMC. Express the bow in inches and in shop "tenths".
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The mating cylinder must clear the wander on both sides, so \( d_{\max}=D-2\delta = 25.010-2(0.008) = 24.994\ \mathrm{mm} \).

(2) The GO plug is 25.000 mm and \( 24.994 < 25.000 \), so it will not enter: the bore is rejected.

(3) The bore micrometer reads 25.010 at every section, and \( 25.000 < 25.010 < 25.021 \), so on that evidence the bore passes — at any number of sections, because the defect is between sections, not in one.

(4) The shaft at MMC is its largest permitted size, 24.993 mm. Clearance is therefore \( 24.994-24.993 = 0.001\ \mathrm{mm} \), against a design minimum of \( 25.000-24.993 = 0.007\ \mathrm{mm} \) — a seventh of what the fit called for.

(5) \( 0.008\ \mathrm{mm}\div25.4 = 0.000315\ \mathrm{in} \), that is 3.15 tenths.

Answer: 24.994 mm effective; GO plug rejects, two-point micrometer passes; 0.001 mm clearance instead of 0.007; the bow is 0.000315 in (3.15 tenths). Sanity check: the two verdicts disagree and the gauge is the one that is right, which is the whole content of Taylor's principle — the GO gauge is a physical model of the mating shaft, and the micrometer is an inference about sections. Note the factor of two: a 0.008 mm bow costs 0.016 mm of usable diameter, so a bow well inside the tolerance can eat the fit entirely. Note also what a shortened, worn-down GO plug would have done here: a stubby pin passes a bent bore easily, and the shop would have lost the only check that saw the fault.

quiz.q:
How far can a process drift before the gauge notices?

Problem. A bore process is normally distributed with a standard deviation of 3.5 µm and is centred in the 25.000 / 25.021 mm tolerance. Find its reject rate when centred, after the mean drifts by one standard deviation, and after two. State what a GO/NO-GO gauge reports at each stage, and find the standard error of the mean of ten measured parts.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The centre is \( (25.000+25.021)/2 = 25.0105 \) mm and the half-width is 0.0105 mm, which is \( 0.0105/0.0035 = 3.0 \) standard deviations. Centred, the reject rate is \( 2\,\Phi(-3) = 2(0.00135) = 0.0027 \), that is 0.27%, one part in 370.

(2) Drifted by \( 1\sigma \), the mean is 25.014. The upper tail is \( z=(25.021-25.014)/0.0035 = 2.0 \rightarrow 0.0228 \); the lower tail is at \( z=4.0 \), worth 0.00003. Total 2.28%, one in 44.

(3) Drifted by \( 2\sigma \), the mean is 25.0175. The upper tail is \( z=1.0 \rightarrow 0.1587 \); the lower is negligible. Total 15.87%, about one in six.

(4) The gauge reports 99.73%, then 97.72%, then 84.13% pass. It reports nothing else, because a pass/fail verdict carries no units and no position within the limits.

(5) \( \mathrm{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt{n} = 0.0035/\sqrt{10} = 0.00111\ \mathrm{mm} = 1.11\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

Answer: 0.27%, 2.28%, 15.87%; the gauge shows 99.73 / 97.72 / 84.13 per cent pass and nothing more; ten measured parts locate the mean to ±1.11 µm. Sanity check: the drift that eventually produced one reject in six was 7 µm, and ten measured parts would have resolved it to about 1 µm — visible long before any part failed. That is the trade the gauge makes: it is faster per part and blind between the limits, so it answers "does this ship?" and cannot answer "where is the process going?". Note also that the reject rate rose almost sixty-fold for a drift of two standard deviations, so the transition from "everything passes" to "a bin of scrap" is abrupt, which is exactly what makes gauge-only inspection feel like a sudden failure rather than a slow one.

quiz.q: A GO plug gauge for a hole specified 25.000 / 25.021 mm is made nominally to
choices: 25.0105 mm, the middle of the tolerance
quiz.solution: The GO gauge always embodies maximum material condition, and for a hole that is the smallest permitted size — most material left. It must enter every acceptable hole, so it has to be as small as the smallest one allowed. For a shaft, MMC is the largest size, so the GO ring gauge is made to the shaft's upper limit instead.

quiz.q: Under Taylor's principle the NO-GO gauge should be
choices: a full-length cylinder, like the GO gauge
short and ideally two-point, checking one section at a time
made to the same size as the GO gauge but hardened differently
used only after the part is assembled
quiz.solution: The least-material limit protects local properties — wall thickness, contact area — so a hole that is oversize anywhere is defective there. A short, two-point NO-GO finds a single oversize section. A full-form NO-GO would jam in a bore that was locally oversize but slightly bent, and the inspector would read the jam as a pass.

quiz.q: The GO gauge must check the whole feature at once because the limit it embodies protects
choices: assembly, which is a property of the whole feature
quiz.solution: MMC exists so that the mating part goes together, and the mating part has to pass along the entire feature rather than through each section separately. That is why the GO gauge is a full-form physical model of the mating part. LMC, by contrast, protects local material, which is why its gauge is local.

quiz.q: A bore measures 25.010 mm at every section but its axis is bowed 0.008 mm. The largest straight cylinder that will pass through it is
quiz.solution: \( d_{\max}=D-2\delta = 25.010-0.016 = 24.994\ \mathrm{mm} \). The mating part must clear the wander on both sides, so a bow costs twice its own value in usable diameter. The common slip is subtracting \( \delta \) once and getting 25.002, which would wrongly pass the bore against a 25.000 GO plug.

quiz.q: Gauge-maker's tolerance disposed entirely inside the work tolerance zone protects
choices: the manufacturer, by widening the accepted band
the customer, by making it impossible for any gauge to accept a part outside its limits
neither party; it is a drafting convention only
the gauge, by reducing its wear rate
quiz.solution: Placing the gauge's own tolerance inside the work zone means that a gauge at the worst end of its tolerance still cannot admit a bad part — the guarantee is complete, and the shop pays for it in lost tolerance. Straddling the work limit instead hands the tolerance back and admits parts up to half the gauge tolerance outside the limit. Both are used; the drawing or the contract should say which.

quiz.q: A wear allowance is applied to
choices: neither, once the gauge is hardened
quiz.solution: The GO gauge enters every part made and wears accordingly; the NO-GO gauge, by design, enters almost none. The allowance is placed so the GO gauge starts on the safe side and wears toward the work limit, at which point it is withdrawn. It is a service-life budget, not permission to keep using a gauge past the limit.

quiz.q: With gauge tolerance at 10% of the work tolerance and a 5% wear allowance, both disposed inward, the band of sizes certain to be accepted is
quiz.solution: The GO end consumes \( t_g + w = 15\% \) and the NO-GO end consumes \( t_g = 10\% \), so \( 25\% \) is lost and \( 0.75\,T \) survives. On the 21 µm hole that is 15.75 µm. The fraction depends only on the two percentages, so it is the same in millimetres or inches and at any nominal size.

quiz.q: A process gauged GO/NO-GO passes essentially everything for weeks, then rejects about one part in six overnight. The most likely explanation is
choices: the mean had been drifting the whole time, and a gauge shows only crossings, not the drift
the tolerance was changed without notice
the operator began measuring more carefully
quiz.solution: A two-standard-deviation drift takes the reject rate from 0.27% to 15.87% while the gauge reports 99.7% then 84.1% pass — and reports nothing in between. The abruptness is an artefact of attribute inspection, not of the process, which moved gradually. Ten measured parts would have located the mean to about 1 µm and shown the drift before anything failed.

5.kuwait:
Applied case — the gauges that were replaced with a better instrument. A machine shop making \( \varnothing25\,\mathrm{H7} \) bores retired its plug gauge sets in favour of a digital bore micrometer, on the reasonable-sounding argument that a number beats a pass. Bore inspection records improved immediately: every part measured between 25.005 and 25.015, well inside 25.000 / 25.021, and the records showed it. Assembly rejects rose over the following weeks, with shafts that would not enter bores the paperwork said were correct.

The bores were bowed. A part that shifts in the fixture during boring produces an axis that wanders while the local diameter stays constant, and a two-point instrument is blind to it by construction — it measures across a section and the defect is between sections. A bore reading 25.010 everywhere with a 0.008 mm bow admits a straight cylinder of only \( 25.010-2(0.008)=24.994\ \mathrm{mm} \). Against a shaft at its MMC of 24.993 that leaves 0.001 mm where the fit was designed for at least 0.007, so the parts assembled by force or not at all. The full-form GO plug had been rejecting these bores all along, and its verdict was discarded as less informative than a number.

Two practices follow. The GO gauge is not a crude substitute for measurement — it is a physical model of the mating part, and for anything that has to assemble it tests a property no set of sectional measurements contains. Where variable data is genuinely wanted for process control, the answer is to measure and gauge, not to swap one for the other. And when an inspection change is followed by more downstream failures, the change is the first suspect, however much better the new records look: the records improved here precisely because the new method could not see the defect.
5.recap:
• A limit gauge is a limit built into steel: the GO gauge embodies maximum material condition, the NO-GO gauge least material condition.
  • For a hole MMC is the smallest permitted size and for a shaft the largest, so a GO plug must enter and a GO ring must pass over.
  • Taylor's principle: the GO gauge checks all dimensions simultaneously over the full length; the NO-GO gauge checks one dimension at a time at individual sections.
  • The reason is functional — MMC protects assembly, which is a whole-feature property, and LMC protects local material.
  • A bowed or lobed bore accepts only \( d_{\max}=D-2\delta \); a 0.008 mm bow in a 25.010 mm bore leaves 24.994 mm, which a full-form GO plug at 25.000 correctly refuses and a two-point micrometer passes at every section.
  • Gauge-maker's tolerance \( t_g=0.10\,T \) and wear allowance \( w=0.05\,T \) are disposed inside the work zone, the wear allowance on the GO gauge only.
  • For the 21 µm hole that gives GO 25.00105 / 25.00315 and NO-GO 25.0189 / 25.0210, and a guaranteed accept band of 15.75 µm — exactly \( 0.75\,T \), the same fraction in inches.
  • The lost quarter is transferred from the manufacturer to the customer; straddling the limit instead hands it back and admits parts up to \( t_g/2 \) outside.
  • Attribute gauging is fast, unambiguous, and makes 100% inspection affordable, and a GO gauge is a more faithful test of a fit than any set of numbers.
  • It is blind between the limits: a \( 2\sigma \) drift takes rejects from 0.27% to 15.87% with no warning, where ten measured parts locate the mean to 1.11 µm. Gauge for the verdict, measure for the process.

6.lecture:
§1 · What is on the surface, and what the instrument does to it

Drag a fine stylus across a machined surface and it traces a profile \( z(x) \). That profile is not one thing. It is a superposition of three, separated by wavelength: form, the intended shape and its long-wavelength errors; waviness, the medium-wavelength undulation left by machine vibration, spindle error or workpiece deflection; and roughness, the short-wavelength marks of the cutting or abrasive process itself.

Nothing in the raw trace announces which is which, so roughness is defined by the filter that extracts it. Two wavelengths do the separating. The long cutoff \( \lambda_c \) divides roughness from waviness; the short cutoff \( \lambda_s \) divides roughness from noise. One sampling length equals \( \lambda_c \), and the standard evaluation length is five of them, so a stated roughness is an average over five sampling lengths.

The instrument filters mechanically before it filters electronically. A stylus tip is a cone ending in a radius, typically 2 µm, and it cannot enter a valley sharper than itself — it bridges across, and the profile it records is smoother than the surface. For a sinusoidal profile of amplitude \( a \) and wavelength \( \lambda \), the radius of curvature at the valley floor is \( \lambda^2/4\pi^2a \), so the tip follows only while that exceeds the tip radius \( r \).

Key relation — the shortest wavelength a stylus can follow

\[ \lambda_{\min}=2\pi\sqrt{a\,r} \]

With \( a=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and a 2 µm tip, \( \lambda_{\min}=6.28\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). A 10 µm feature is traced faithfully; a 4 µm one is bridged and under-reported.

This is worth stating plainly because it is the honest version of a claim instruments make about themselves: a 0.01 µm vertical resolution says nothing about whether the tip reached the bottom of the valley it was resolving. Optical instruments trade this problem for different ones — they have no tip radius, but steep flanks scatter light away and are reported as missing data.

§2 · Ra, Rz, Rq, and what each of them discards

From the filtered profile, taken about its mean line, the standard parameters follow.

Key relations — the amplitude parameters

\[ R_a=\frac{1}{L}\int_0^L|z|\,dx,\qquad R_q=\sqrt{\frac{1}{L}\int_0^L z^2\,dx},\qquad R_z=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^{5}\bigl(z_{p,i}-z_{v,i}\bigr) \]

\( R_a \) is the mean magnitude of the deviation, \( R_q \) its root mean square, and \( R_z \) the mean of the five largest peak-to-valley heights, one from each sampling length. \( R_t \) is the single largest peak-to-valley height over the whole evaluation length.

\( R_a \) dominates drawings because it is stable: it averages over the whole trace, so a stray scratch barely moves it, and repeat measurements agree. That stability is also its defect. It is blind to shape, and shape is what most surfaces are for.

The diagram makes the point with two profiles of identical \( R_a=0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The first is a sinusoid, which needs amplitude \( a=\pi R_a/2=1.257\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and so stands 2.51 µm crest to trough. The second is plateau-honed: flat over 90% of its length with narrow valleys of depth \( d \). Its mean line sits \( 0.1d \) below the plateau, so \( R_a=0.9(0.1d)+0.1(0.9d)=0.18d \), giving \( d=4.44\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) — 1.77 times the total height of the sinusoid, at the same \( R_a \).

The cheapest discriminator is the ratio \( R_q/R_a \), because \( R_q \) weights large deviations by their square and \( R_a \) does not. A sinusoid gives \( \pi/2\sqrt2=1.111 \); a random surface with a normal height distribution gives \( \sqrt{\pi/2}=1.253 \); the plateau profile above gives 1.667. A measured ratio well above 1.25 says the height distribution has a tail — deep valleys, or high peaks, and the sign of the skew says which. When that distinction actually governs function, the standard offers parameters built for it (\( R_k \), \( R_{pk} \), \( R_{vk} \), from the bearing-area curve), and a drawing that cares should call for them rather than tightening \( R_a \) and hoping.

§3 · Why the cutoff changes the answer

Because roughness is whatever survives the filter, changing \( \lambda_c \) changes the measured value on an unchanged surface. This is not instrument error. It is the definition working.

Take a profile that is the sum of two sinusoids: a machining roughness of 0.5 µm amplitude at 0.1 mm wavelength, and a waviness of 2.0 µm amplitude at 1.6 mm. Measured with \( \lambda_c=0.8\ \mathrm{mm} \), the 1.6 mm component is longer than the cutoff and is removed as waviness, leaving \( R_a=2(0.5)/\pi=0.318\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Measured with \( \lambda_c=2.5\ \mathrm{mm} \), the 1.6 mm component is shorter than the cutoff, survives as roughness, and \( R_a=1.294\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The same surface, the same instrument, the same operator: 4.06 times the answer.

Key rule — a roughness figure without its cutoff is not a specification

\[ R_a \text{ alone is incomplete};\qquad R_a\ \text{with}\ \lambda_c\ \text{is a number} \]

The standard cutoff is chosen from the roughness itself — 0.8 mm for \( R_a \) between 0.1 and 2 µm, 2.5 mm above that, 0.25 mm below − so a first trace is used to pick the cutoff for the second.

That selection rule sounds circular and is not: it is a two-pass procedure, and it exists so that the filter is matched to the process rather than to the inspector. The practical consequences are direct. A supplier and a customer measuring the same part with different cutoffs will disagree by a factor, and neither will be wrong. A drawing calling for \( R_a\ 0.8 \) with no cutoff has under-specified the part. And a surface whose real content sits near the cutoff — a milled face with feed marks at roughly \( \lambda_c \) — is the case where the disagreement is worst, because the filter is cutting exactly where the energy is.

The same logic governs the short end. \( \lambda_s \) exists so that electrical noise and the stylus's own tip effects are not reported as roughness, and it is the reason a measured profile should never be read as the true surface at scales near the tip radius.

§4 · Matching a finish to what the surface has to do

A finish specification is a functional requirement, not a quality aspiration, and smoother is frequently wrong. Four cases cover most of what an engineer specifies.

A face that has to seal against a soft gasket wants texture, not polish. A spiral-wound or compressed-fibre gasket seats by biting into the flange face, and a lapped flange gives it nothing to grip; the usual call is a controlled serrated or phonographic finish in the \( R_a\ 3.2\text{--}6.3\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) range. A face that has to seal against a rigid counterface — a mechanical seal, a metal-to-metal joint — is the opposite: the leak path is the roughness itself, so it is lapped to \( R_a\ 0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) or better, and flatness is checked optically rather than by stylus. A surface that is going to be painted or bonded wants tooth for the adhesive to key into, so a blasted or coarsely machined \( R_a\ 3.2\text{--}12.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) is specified deliberately. A lubricated sliding surface is the interesting one, because it wants both: a smooth load-carrying plateau and valleys deep enough to hold oil — which is the plateau-honed profile of §2, and exactly what \( R_a \) alone cannot specify.

Key relation — the film-thickness ratio

\[ \Lambda=\frac{h_{\min}}{\sqrt{R_{q,1}^2+R_{q,2}^2}} \]

Roughnesses of two contacting surfaces combine in quadrature. \( \Lambda>3 \) is full-film separation, \( 1<\Lambda<3 \) is mixed lubrication with intermittent asperity contact, and \( \Lambda<1 \) is boundary contact. The film thickness \( h_{\min} \) comes from the bearing analysis; the roughnesses come from this lesson.

A journal at \( R_q=0.25\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) running in a shell at \( R_q=0.40 \) has a composite roughness of \( \sqrt{0.25^2+0.40^2}=0.472\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). With a minimum film of 1.8 µm, \( \Lambda=3.82 \) — the surfaces never touch. Refinish the journal to \( R_q=0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and the composite becomes 0.894, so \( \Lambda=2.01 \): the film is unchanged, the clearance is unchanged, the drawing dimensions are unchanged, and the bearing is now in mixed lubrication, where it will wear. The only thing that moved was a finish, and the number that governed it was \( R_q \) rather than \( R_a \).

Two habits follow from all of this. State the cutoff with the roughness, always, or the specification does not close. And say what the surface is for — a finish specified for a seal face, a gasket seat and a paint key are three different requirements that a single tightened \( R_a \) serves badly.

quiz.q:
Two surfaces, one Ra

Problem. Surface A is sinusoidal with \( R_a=0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Surface B is plateau-honed: flat over 90% of its length, with valleys of depth \( d \) over the remaining 10%, and it too measures \( R_a=0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Find the total height \( R_t \) of each and the ratio \( R_q/R_a \) of each, and say which parameter would have distinguished them on a drawing.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) For a sinusoid of amplitude \( a \), \( R_a = 2a/\pi \), so \( a = \pi(0.80)/2 = 1.257\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and \( R_t = 2a = 2.513\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) \( R_q = a/\sqrt2 = 0.889\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so \( R_q/R_a = \pi/(2\sqrt2) = 1.111 \).

(3) For surface B the mean line must pass through the profile's centroid. With the plateau at height 0 and the valleys at \( -d \), the mean sits at \( -0.1d \), so the plateau is \( +0.1d \) above it and the valley floor \( -0.9d \) below.

(4) \( R_a = 0.9(0.1d) + 0.1(0.9d) = 0.18d \). Setting this to 0.80 gives \( d = 4.444\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), which is \( R_t \) — 1.77 times surface A's.

(5) \( R_q^2 = 0.9(0.1d)^2 + 0.1(0.9d)^2 = 0.09d^2 \), so \( R_q = 0.3d = 1.333\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and \( R_q/R_a = 0.3d/0.18d = 1.667 \).

(6) \( R_a \) is identical, so it distinguishes nothing. \( R_t \) or \( R_z \) separates them by 1.77 times, and \( R_q/R_a \) separates them as 1.111 against 1.667.

Answer: A: \( R_t=2.51\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), \( R_q/R_a=1.111 \). B: \( R_t=4.44\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), \( R_q/R_a=1.667 \). \( R_a \) cannot tell them apart; a peak-to-valley parameter or the \( R_q/R_a \) ratio can. Sanity check: a random surface with a normal height distribution gives \( R_q/R_a=\sqrt{\pi/2}=1.253 \), so both results sit either side of that benchmark in the right direction — the sinusoid has no tail and reads low, the valley-dominated profile has a long one and reads high. Note the practical inversion: surface B is the rougher by every extreme measure and is the better bearing surface, because it carries load on 90% of its area and stores oil in the rest.

quiz.q:
The same surface, two cutoffs

Problem. A profile is the sum of two sinusoids: 0.5 µm amplitude at 0.1 mm wavelength, and 2.0 µm amplitude at 1.6 mm. Give \( R_q \) as measured with \( \lambda_c=0.8\ \mathrm{mm} \) and with \( \lambda_c=2.5\ \mathrm{mm} \), and the ratio between them. State which reading a drawing calling for "\( R_a\ 0.4 \)" would have been judged against.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) A long cutoff \( \lambda_c \) passes wavelengths shorter than itself as roughness and rejects longer ones as waviness.

(2) At \( \lambda_c=0.8 \) mm: the 0.1 mm component passes, the 1.6 mm component is rejected because \( 1.6 > 0.8 \). Only the roughness survives, and for a single sinusoid \( R_q = a/\sqrt2 = 0.5/\sqrt2 = 0.354\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) At \( \lambda_c=2.5 \) mm: both components pass, since \( 1.6 < 2.5 \). Sinusoids of different wavelength are orthogonal over a common length, so their mean squares add: \( R_q = \sqrt{a_1^2/2 + a_2^2/2} = \sqrt{0.125+2.000} = \sqrt{2.125} = 1.458\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(4) The ratio is \( 1.458/0.354 = 4.12 \). (The corresponding \( R_a \) values are 0.318 and 1.294 µm, a factor of 4.06 — the same story.)

(5) The 0.8 mm cutoff is the standard choice for \( R_a \) between 0.1 and 2 µm, so a drawing calling for \( R_a\ 0.4 \) with no cutoff stated would be judged against 0.318 and the part would pass — while an inspector who chose 2.5 mm would read 1.294 and reject it.

Answer: \( R_q = 0.354\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at \( \lambda_c=0.8 \) mm and \( 1.458\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at 2.5 mm, a factor of 4.12; the part passes on one cutoff and fails on the other. Sanity check: nothing about the surface changed, so this is the definition of roughness showing itself, not a measurement error — roughness is what survives the filter. Note that the waviness carries almost all the height here \( (2.0 \) against \( 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}) \), which is why including it swamps the result; a surface whose waviness were small would show little cutoff sensitivity. This is the whole reason a specification without \( \lambda_c \) is incomplete.

quiz.q:
A refinished journal, and a US customary check

Problem. A journal finished to \( R_q=0.25\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) runs in a shell at \( R_q=0.40\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) with a minimum oil film of 1.8 µm. Find the film-thickness ratio and classify the lubrication regime. The journal is later reground to \( R_q=0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) with everything else unchanged; repeat. Express both journal finishes in micro-inches.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The two roughnesses combine in quadrature: \( \sigma = \sqrt{0.25^2+0.40^2} = \sqrt{0.0625+0.1600} = \sqrt{0.2225} = 0.472\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) \( \Lambda = h_{\min}/\sigma = 1.8/0.472 = 3.82 \). Since \( \Lambda > 3 \), the surfaces are fully separated by the film and do not touch.

(3) After regrinding, \( \sigma = \sqrt{0.80^2+0.40^2} = \sqrt{0.80} = 0.894\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(4) \( \Lambda = 1.8/0.894 = 2.01 \), which is between 1 and 3: mixed lubrication, with asperities touching through the film.

(5) \( 0.25\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 250/25.4 = 9.8\ \mu\mathrm{in} \) and \( 0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 800/25.4 = 31.5\ \mu\mathrm{in} \).

Answer: \( \Lambda = 3.82 \) (full film) before, \( \Lambda = 2.01 \) (mixed) after; the journal went from 9.8 to 31.5 micro-inches. Sanity check: the clearance, the oil, the load and every dimension on the drawing were unchanged — only a finish moved, and the bearing crossed out of full-film operation into a regime where it wears. That is why a journal drawing states a finish at all, and why the parameter it should state is \( R_q \): the quadrature sum is a sum of squares, so it is \( R_q \) that combines correctly and \( R_a \) that does not. Note the rougher surface dominates the composite — at 0.80 against 0.40, the shell contributes only a tenth of \( \sigma^2 \), so polishing the shell would have bought almost nothing.

quiz.q: Roughness is separated from waviness by
choices: the vertical resolution of the instrument
quiz.solution: \( \lambda_c \) is the wavelength at which the filter divides them: shorter content is reported as roughness, longer as waviness. One sampling length equals \( \lambda_c \) and the evaluation length is five of them. The tip radius and \( \lambda_s \) act at the short end, keeping noise and tip artefacts out.

quiz.q: The same surface measured at \( \lambda_c = 0.8 \) mm and at \( \lambda_c = 2.5 \) mm gives \( R_a \) values differing by a factor of four. This means
choices: the surface has substantial content between those two wavelengths, and both readings are correct
the longer cutoff is always wrong
quiz.solution: Both are correct measurements of different quantities, because roughness is defined as what survives the filter. Here a 1.6 mm undulation is waviness at the 0.8 mm cutoff and roughness at the 2.5 mm cutoff. It is why a roughness value quoted without its cutoff is not a specification, and why supplier and customer can disagree by a factor with neither at fault.

quiz.q: Two surfaces both measure \( R_a = 0.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). One is sinusoidal, the other plateau-honed with deep valleys. Their \( R_q/R_a \) ratios are
quiz.solution: \( R_q \) weights deviations by their square, so a profile with deep valleys raises \( R_q \) without raising \( R_a \) proportionately: 1.111 for the sinusoid, 1.667 for the plateau profile. A random surface with a normal height distribution sits at \( \sqrt{\pi/2}=1.253 \), so the ratio is a quick test for whether the height distribution has a tail.

quiz.q: A 2 µm stylus tip traversing a profile of 0.5 µm amplitude will bridge rather than follow features shorter than about
quiz.solution: \( \lambda_{\min}=2\pi\sqrt{ar}=2\pi\sqrt{(0.5)(2)}=6.28\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Below that the valley floor is sharper than the tip and the recorded profile is smoother than the real surface. A quoted vertical resolution of 0.01 µm says nothing about this — the limit is geometric, not electrical.

quiz.q: A flange face that must seal against a spiral-wound gasket should be specified
choices: as smooth as the shop can lap it
with a controlled texture around \( R_a\ 3.2\text{--}6.3\ \mu\mathrm{m} \)
with no finish requirement, since the gasket does the sealing
the same as a mechanical seal face
quiz.solution: A soft gasket seals by biting into the face, so it needs something to grip; a lapped flange gives it nothing and can leak. The controlled serrated finish is a functional requirement in its own right. The opposite case — a rigid counterface such as a mechanical seal, where the roughness is the leak path — is lapped to 0.1 µm or better.

quiz.q: Two surfaces with \( R_q \) of 0.25 and 0.40 µm have a composite roughness of
quiz.solution: They combine in quadrature: \( \sqrt{0.25^2+0.40^2}=\sqrt{0.2225}=0.472\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), not by addition. Because it is a sum of squares, the rougher surface dominates — and because it is a sum of squares, the parameter that combines correctly is \( R_q \) rather than \( R_a \).

quiz.q: A bearing operating at \( \Lambda = 2.0 \) is in
choices: full-film separation, with no asperity contact
mixed lubrication, with intermittent asperity contact
quiz.solution: \( \Lambda>3 \) is full film, \( 1<\Lambda<3 \) is mixed, \( \Lambda<1 \) is boundary. At 2.0 the film carries most of the load but asperities touch, and the surface wears. In the worked example the bearing arrived there purely by being refinished coarser — the film, clearance and load were unchanged.

quiz.q: The main reason \( R_a \) dominates drawings despite being blind to profile shape is
choices: it is the only parameter most instruments compute
it averages over the whole trace, so it is reproducible and insensitive to a stray scratch
it is the largest of the amplitude parameters
it does not require a cutoff to be stated
quiz.solution: Averaging magnitudes over the evaluation length makes \( R_a \) stable and repeatable, which is a real virtue in a shop specification. The cost is that it discards shape entirely. Every instrument computes \( R_q \) and \( R_z \) as well, \( R_t \) is larger by construction, and \( R_a \) needs a cutoff exactly like the others.

6.kuwait:
Applied case — the polished journal that wore out. A pump shaft came back from an overhaul with its journals reground and then polished, on the instruction "improve the finish". The shop measured them, recorded \( R_a\ 0.35\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) against a drawing calling for 0.4 maximum, and released the shaft. The bearings wore visibly within a few hundred hours.

The measurement was in specification and the surface was wrong. Polishing had removed the honing valleys and left a smooth, near-sinusoidal profile: same \( R_a \), \( R_q \) risen from 0.25 to about 0.4 µm as the profile lost its plateau character, and — the part that mattered — no valleys left to hold oil where the film thins at start-up and shutdown. On top of that the drawing specified only \( R_a \) with no cutoff and no shape parameter, so the finish that had worked for years was never actually specified; it had been produced by the original honing process and preserved by habit.

Two practices follow. Where the surface has a job beyond looking finished, specify the parameter that governs that job — \( R_q \) for a lubricated contact, a peak-to-valley or bearing-area parameter where oil retention or contact area is the point — and state the cutoff so the number closes. And treat "improve the finish" as an unsafe instruction on a functional surface: it is a direction without a target, and on a plateau-honed journal the improvement runs the wrong way.
6.recap:
• A stylus trace contains form, waviness and roughness together; roughness is defined by the filter that extracts it, so it does not exist independently of \( \lambda_c \).
  • One sampling length is \( \lambda_c \) and the standard evaluation length is \( 5\lambda_c \).
  • The stylus filters mechanically before anything electronic does: it follows only wavelengths longer than \( \lambda_{\min}=2\pi\sqrt{ar} \), which is 6.3 µm for a 2 µm tip on a 0.5 µm amplitude.
  • \( R_a \) is the mean magnitude, \( R_q \) the root mean square, \( R_z \) and \( R_t \) the peak-to-valley measures.
  • \( R_a \) is stable and blind to shape: a sinusoid and a plateau-honed profile both at 0.80 µm stand 2.51 and 4.44 µm tall, a factor of 1.77.
  • \( R_q/R_a \) is the cheapest discriminator — 1.111 for a sinusoid, 1.253 for a random normal surface, 1.667 for the plateau profile.
  • Changing the cutoff changes the answer on an unchanged surface: 0.5 µm at 0.1 mm plus 2.0 µm at 1.6 mm reads \( R_a\ 0.318 \) at \( \lambda_c = 0.8 \) mm and 1.294 at 2.5 mm, a factor of 4.06.
  • A roughness value quoted without its cutoff is not a specification, and two parties can disagree by a factor with neither at fault.
  • Finish is a functional requirement: texture for a soft gasket, lapped for a rigid counterface, tooth for paint or adhesive, plateau with valleys for a lubricated slide.
  • \( \Lambda = h_{\min}/\sqrt{R_{q,1}^2+R_{q,2}^2} \) — a journal refinished from \( R_q\ 0.25 \) to 0.80 µm takes \( \Lambda \) from 3.82 to 2.01, out of full film and into mixed lubrication, with nothing else on the drawing changed.

7.lecture:
§1 · Two kinds of variation, and why the response differs

Every process varies. The whole of statistical process control rests on one distinction, due to Shewhart: some of that variation belongs to the process and some does not.

Common-cause variation is the sum of many small influences that are always present — tool wear between regrinds, coolant temperature, material hardness within its own specification, the operator's loading. No single one is identifiable, and together they produce a stable, predictable distribution. Special-cause variation comes from something assignable that is not part of the system: a tool has chipped, a batch of material is different, a fixture has loosened, a new operator is running the machine.

The two demand opposite responses, and this is the practical point. A special cause should be found and removed — it is an event, it has a story, and the story is usually short. A common cause should be left alone at the machine and attacked at the system level, because there is no single thing to fix and adjusting for it makes the output worse. Not slightly worse: measurably worse.

Key result — the cost of tampering

\[ \sigma^2_{\text{adjusted}}=2\sigma^2,\qquad \sigma_{\text{adjusted}}=\sqrt2\,\sigma\approx1.414\,\sigma \]

Adjusting the machine by \( -(x_n-T) \) after every part gives \( x_{n+1}=T-e_n+e_{n+1} \), the difference of two independent errors. The variance doubles and the standard deviation rises by 41%.

The derivation is worth following because the result is so counter-intuitive to anyone standing at a machine. Let the uncontrolled output be \( x_n=T+a_n+e_n \), where \( a_n \) is the current offset and \( e_n \) is an independent random error with standard deviation \( \sigma \). The conscientious operator sets \( a_{n+1}=a_n-(x_n-T)=-e_n \). The next part is then \( x_{n+1}=T-e_n+e_{n+1} \), which has variance \( \sigma^2+\sigma^2 \). Every correction was sensible, every one was made in good faith, and the process got 41% worse. This is tampering, and it is the commonest way a shop makes a stable process unstable.

So the first question about any deviation is not "how do I correct it?" but "is this the process talking, or something new?" A control chart exists to answer exactly that question and nothing else.

§2 · Building an \( \bar{X} \)–\( R \) chart

Take small samples of consecutive parts — a rational subgroup, usually four or five — at intervals. Consecutive matters: the subgroup must be chosen so that only common causes can act within it, leaving any special cause to show up between subgroups. A subgroup made of one part from each of five machines destroys the method before it starts.

From each subgroup take the mean \( \bar{X} \) and the range \( R \). Average those over a baseline of twenty or so subgroups to get \( \bar{\bar{X}} \) and \( \bar{R} \), and the limits follow.

Key relations — the chart limits

\[ \hat\sigma=\frac{\bar R}{d_2},\qquad \bar{\bar X}\pm A_2\bar R\ \text{ with }\ A_2=\frac{3}{d_2\sqrt n},\qquad \text{UCL}_R=D_4\bar R,\ \ \text{LCL}_R=D_3\bar R \]

At \( n=5 \): \( d_2=2.326 \), so \( A_2=3/(2.326\sqrt5)=0.577 \), and \( D_4=2.114 \), \( D_3=0 \). The limits are three standard errors of the mean, nothing more exotic — \( A_2 \) simply packages \( 3/(d_2\sqrt n) \) so the shop never has to compute \( \hat\sigma \).

The chart in the diagram uses ten subgroups of five bores, measured in micrometres above 25.000 mm. The first eight are the baseline: \( \bar{\bar X}=10.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and \( \bar R=4.25\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so \( A_2\bar R=0.577(4.25)=2.45 \) and the limits are 7.75 and 12.65 µm. The range chart's upper limit is \( 2.114(4.25)=8.98\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

Read the range chart first, always. It reports the process spread, and the \( \bar{X} \) limits are computed from \( \bar R \) — so if the spread is unstable, the \( \bar{X} \) limits were built on sand and mean nothing. Here every range from 3 to 6 µm sits well inside 8.98, so the spread is stable and the \( \bar{X} \) chart can be trusted. Subgroup 9 then reads 13.1, above the upper control limit, while its range is an unremarkable 5. A signal on the mean with no signal on the range says the process level shifted and its spread did not — which points at a setting, an offset, a new batch, not at a worn tool or a loose fixture.

The estimate that falls out of the same arithmetic is \( \hat\sigma=\bar R/d_2=4.25/2.326=1.83\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so the process's own spread is \( 6\hat\sigma=10.96\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) against a 21 µm tolerance — it occupies about half of what it was given. Comparing those two numbers properly is the next lesson's subject.

§3 · Control limits are not specification limits

This is the confusion that ruins more charts than any other, and it is worth stating as bluntly as possible.

Key distinction

Control limits are computed from the process and describe what it does. They apply to a subgroup statistic, and on an \( \bar{X} \) chart they sit at \( \pm3\sigma/\sqrt n \).

Specification limits are set by the designer and describe what is wanted. They apply to an individual part. They are never computed, never plotted on an \( \bar{X} \) chart, and never used to judge whether a process is stable.

The arithmetic shows why mixing them is not a matter of taste. With \( n=5 \) the control limits sit at \( \pm3\sigma/\sqrt5=\pm1.34\sigma \) — less than half the \( \pm3\sigma \) spread of the individual parts. On the worked chart that is \( \pm2.45\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) about the centre line for the means, against \( \pm5.48\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) for single bores. The specification limits are at −10.2 and +10.8 µm from the same centre. Draw them on the \( \bar{X} \) chart, as the diagram does deliberately, and they are so far out that no realistic shift would ever reach them: the chart would signal nothing until the process had been producing scrap for a long time.

Two statements follow that sound like paradoxes and are not. A process can be in perfect statistical control and produce nothing but scrap — control means predictable, not good, and a stable process centred outside the tolerance is stably wrong. And a process can sit comfortably inside the tolerance while being wildly out of control — there is room to wander, and it is wandering, and the day it wanders past the edge nothing on the chart will have warned anyone.

Those are the two independent questions a shop has to keep separate: is it stable?, which the control chart answers, and is it good enough?, which the tolerance answers. A chart with specification limits drawn on it has silently merged them and answers neither.

§4 · Reading the chart, and the two errors on offer

The basic signal is a point beyond a control limit. With limits at three standard errors and a stable normal process, the chance a point falls outside by luck alone is \( 2(1-\Phi(3))=0.0027 \), so the average run length between false alarms is \( 1/0.0027=370 \) subgroups. That is the number the three-sigma convention was chosen to produce: rare enough that a signal is worth acting on.

Rare per point is not rare per chart. Over 25 in-control points the chance of at least one false alarm is \( 1-(1-0.0027)^{25}=6.5\% \), and a shop running several charts sees false alarms routinely. Supplementary runs rules — eight consecutive points on one side of the centre line, two of three beyond two standard errors — catch small sustained shifts that the beyond-limit rule misses, at the price of more false alarms still: eight in a row on one side has probability \( 2(0.5)^8=0.0078 \) by chance alone.

Key relation — how fast a shift is caught

\[ P_{\text{detect}}=1-\Phi\!\left(3-k\sqrt n\right)+\Phi\!\left(-3-k\sqrt n\right), \qquad \mathrm{ARL}=\frac{1}{P_{\text{detect}}} \]

for a shift of \( k \) process standard deviations. The subgroup size enters as \( \sqrt n \), which is the whole reason subgroups exist.

With \( n=5 \), a shift of one standard deviation is detected with probability 0.222 per subgroup, an average run length of 4.5 subgroups. A shift of two is detected with probability 0.930 — an average run length of 1.08, essentially the next point. Small shifts are slow to find and large ones are immediate, and the leverage is in \( \sqrt n \): moving from \( n=1 \) to \( n=5 \) is what turns a one-sigma shift from nearly invisible into a four-subgroup wait.

Behind all of it are two errors with different costs. Treating common cause as special is tampering, and §1 priced it at a 41% rise in the standard deviation. Treating special cause as common is missing a real event while it is still cheap to fix, and leaving it in the process until it becomes the new normal. The chart is not a scoreboard; it is an instrument for telling those two mistakes apart, and its only output is a decision about which kind of variation just occurred.

quiz.q:
Build the chart, in millimetres and then in inches

Problem. Eight baseline subgroups of five bores give \( \bar{\bar X}=10.2\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) above 25.000 mm and \( \bar R=4.25\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Derive \( A_2 \) from \( d_2=2.326 \) rather than quoting it, and give the \( \bar X \) and \( R \) chart limits and the estimated process standard deviation. Then state whether a ninth subgroup with \( \bar X=13.1 \) and \( R=5 \) is a signal, and what kind. Finally, repeat the \( \bar X \) limits for a shaft process with \( \bar{\bar X}=1.24980 \) in and \( \bar R=0.00042 \) in.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The control limits are three standard errors of the mean, and \( \hat\sigma=\bar R/d_2 \), so \( 3\hat\sigma/\sqrt n = 3\bar R/(d_2\sqrt n) \). Hence \( A_2 = 3/(d_2\sqrt n) = 3/(2.326\sqrt5) = 3/5.2011 = 0.577 \).

(2) \( A_2\bar R = 0.577(4.25) = 2.452\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so \( \mathrm{UCL}=10.2+2.452=12.65 \) and \( \mathrm{LCL}=10.2-2.452=7.75\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) \( \mathrm{UCL}_R = D_4\bar R = 2.114(4.25) = 8.98\ \mu\mathrm{m} \); \( D_3=0 \) at \( n=5 \), so \( \mathrm{LCL}_R = 0 \).

(4) \( \hat\sigma = 4.25/2.326 = 1.83\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so the process spread is \( 6\hat\sigma = 10.96\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). As a check, \( 3\hat\sigma/\sqrt5 = 2.451 \), which matches \( A_2\bar R = 2.452 \) to the rounding in \( A_2 \).

(5) Subgroup 9: \( \bar X = 13.1 > 12.65 \), so the \( \bar X \) chart signals. Its range, 5 µm, is well inside 8.98, so the \( R \) chart does not. A signal on the mean alone means the process level shifted while its spread was unchanged.

(6) In inches: \( \hat\sigma = 0.00042/2.326 = 0.000181 \) in; \( A_2\bar R = 0.577(0.00042) = 0.000242 \) in; limits \( 1.24980\pm0.000242 \), that is 1.249558 and 1.250042 in.

Answer: \( A_2=0.577 \); \( \bar X \) limits 7.75 / 12.65 µm, \( R \) limits 0 / 8.98 µm, \( \hat\sigma=1.83\ \mu\mathrm{m} \); subgroup 9 is a level shift, not a spread change; the inch chart runs 1.249558 to 1.250042 in. Sanity check: \( A_2 \) is not a magic table entry — it is \( 3/(d_2\sqrt n) \), and recovering 0.577 from 2.326 and \( \sqrt5 \) confirms the limits really are three standard errors. Note the order of reading: the \( \bar X \) limits are built from \( \bar R \), so an unstable range chart would make them meaningless, which is why the range chart is read first. Note also that the two unit systems needed no separate theory — every constant is dimensionless.

quiz.q:
What the conscientious operator costs

Problem. A stable process produces \( x_n = T + a_n + e_n \), where \( T \) is the target, \( a_n \) the current machine offset and \( e_n \) an independent error with standard deviation \( \sigma \). After each part the operator resets the offset by \( a_{n+1} = a_n - (x_n - T) \). Find the variance of the output under this policy, and the percentage change in the standard deviation. State what the operator should have done instead, and how a control chart would have told them.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Substituting the observation into the adjustment rule, \( a_{n+1} = a_n - (a_n + e_n) = -e_n \). The offset becomes exactly the negative of the last error.

(2) The next part is therefore \( x_{n+1} = T + a_{n+1} + e_{n+1} = T - e_n + e_{n+1} \).

(3) The two errors are independent, so their variances add: \( \operatorname{Var}(x_{n+1}) = \sigma^2 + \sigma^2 = 2\sigma^2 \).

(4) The standard deviation becomes \( \sqrt2\,\sigma = 1.414\sigma \), a rise of 41.4%.

(5) The correct action is to leave the machine alone: the deviations were common-cause, and a process in control is already doing the best it can without changing the system. A control chart would have shown every one of those readings inside the limits, which is precisely the instruction "do not adjust".

Answer: the variance doubles to \( 2\sigma^2 \) and the standard deviation rises 41.4%; the operator should have made no adjustment, and an in-control chart is what says so. Sanity check: nothing in the derivation depends on \( \sigma \), the target or the machine, so tampering costs the same 41% on any stable process — it is a property of the feedback rule, not of the equipment. Note that every individual correction was reasonable and made in good faith, which is why the result has to be derived rather than argued: intuition at the machine says each adjustment reduced an error, and the arithmetic says the corrections were adding a second independent error to every part.

quiz.q:
How long before the chart notices?

Problem. An \( \bar X \) chart uses subgroups of five and three-sigma limits. Find the false-alarm probability per point and the in-control average run length, and the probability of at least one false alarm in 25 in-control points. Then find the probability of detecting a shift of one process standard deviation on any single subgroup, and of two, with the corresponding average run lengths. Comment on what changing \( n \) would do.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) In control, a point falls outside three standard errors with probability \( 2(1-\Phi(3)) = 2(0.00135) = 0.0027 \).

(2) \( \mathrm{ARL}_0 = 1/0.0027 = 370 \) subgroups between false alarms.

(3) Over 25 points, \( P = 1-(1-0.0027)^{25} = 1-0.9347 = 0.065 \), about one chart in fifteen.

(4) A shift of \( k \) process standard deviations moves the mean by \( k\sqrt n \) standard errors, so \( P = 1-\Phi(3-k\sqrt n)+\Phi(-3-k\sqrt n) \). For \( k=1 \), \( n=5 \): \( 1-\Phi(3-2.236) = 1-\Phi(0.764) = 0.222 \), and the lower tail adds nothing. ARL \( = 1/0.222 = 4.5 \) subgroups.

(5) For \( k=2 \): \( 1-\Phi(3-4.472) = 1-\Phi(-1.472) = 0.930 \), so ARL \( = 1.08 \) — essentially the next subgroup.

(6) \( n \) enters only as \( \sqrt n \). Doubling the subgroup to 10 makes \( k\sqrt n = 3.162 \) for a one-sigma shift, raising detection to \( 1-\Phi(-0.162)=0.564 \) and dropping the ARL to 1.8 — at twice the measuring cost per subgroup.

Answer: 0.0027 per point, \( \mathrm{ARL}_0 = 370 \), 6.5% over 25 points; detection 0.222 (ARL 4.5) for a \( 1\sigma \) shift and 0.930 (ARL 1.08) for \( 2\sigma \); sensitivity scales as \( \sqrt n \). Sanity check: the in-control ARL of 370 is what the three-sigma convention was chosen to deliver — a false alarm rare enough to be worth investigating. The 6.5% over 25 points is the same number read the other way and explains why a shop running several charts sees false alarms regularly; it is not evidence the charts are wrong. Note the asymmetry that matters in practice: big shifts are caught immediately and small ones are slow, which is exactly why runs rules exist and why they buy their extra sensitivity with extra false alarms.

quiz.q: An operator adjusts the machine by the full deviation after every part. Compared with leaving it alone, the output standard deviation
quiz.solution: The adjustment makes the offset \( -e_n \), so the next part carries \( -e_n+e_{n+1} \): two independent errors instead of one, variance \( 2\sigma^2 \), standard deviation \( \sqrt2\,\sigma \) — 41% worse. The result depends only on the feedback rule, not on the machine or the size of \( \sigma \).

quiz.q: On an \( \bar X \)–\( R \) chart pair, the range chart should be read first because
choices: the \( \bar X \) limits are computed from \( \bar R \), so an unstable spread invalidates them
the range is more precise than the mean
quiz.solution: \( \bar{\bar X}\pm A_2\bar R \) takes its width entirely from \( \bar R \). If the spread is unstable, \( \bar R \) is not estimating anything and the \( \bar X \) limits were built on sand. The mean chart, not the range chart, is the faster detector of a level shift.

quiz.q: The constant \( A_2 = 0.577 \) at \( n = 5 \) is
choices: an empirical factor with no derivation
the ratio of the range to the standard deviation
three standard deviations of a single part
quiz.solution: \( A_2 \) packages three standard errors of the mean expressed through the range: \( 3\hat\sigma/\sqrt n = 3\bar R/(d_2\sqrt n) \). At \( n=5 \), \( 3/(2.326\sqrt5)=0.577 \). It exists so the shop never has to compute \( \hat\sigma \), not because the limits are anything other than three standard errors.

quiz.q: A subgroup mean falls outside the \( \bar X \) limits while the range chart stays in control. This points to
choices: a change in the process spread
a shift in the process level
a specification that is too tight
quiz.solution: The two charts separate level from spread. A mean-only signal says the process moved without becoming more variable — a setting, an offset, a new batch of material — rather than a worn tool or a loose fixture, which would widen the ranges. Specification limits play no part in either chart.

quiz.q: Control limits and specification limits differ in that
choices: specification limits are recomputed as the process changes
control limits are computed from the process and apply to a subgroup statistic; specification limits are set by the designer and apply to a part
they are the same thing expressed in different units
quiz.solution: One describes what the process does, the other what is wanted, and they apply to different quantities — a subgroup mean against a single part. On an \( \bar X \) chart at \( n=5 \) the control limits sit at \( \pm1.34\sigma \) while individual parts spread over \( \pm3\sigma \), so specification limits drawn on the same chart sit far outside and the chart signals nothing.

quiz.q: A process is in perfect statistical control. It follows that
choices: the process is predictable, which says nothing about whether it meets the specification
the specification limits equal the control limits
quiz.solution: Control means stable and predictable, not good. A process centred outside its tolerance can be in flawless control and produce nothing but scrap — stably wrong. The converse also holds: a process can sit inside the tolerance while wandering badly, with no warning on the day it wanders out.

quiz.q: With three-sigma limits, the average run length between false alarms on an in-control chart is about
quiz.solution: \( 2(1-\Phi(3)) = 0.0027 \) per point, so \( \mathrm{ARL}_0 = 1/0.0027 = 370 \). That is the number the three-sigma convention was chosen to produce. Read the other way, 25 points carry a 6.5% chance of at least one false alarm, which is why a shop with several charts sees them regularly.

quiz.q: At \( n = 5 \), an \( \bar X \) chart detects a shift of one process standard deviation with probability about 0.22 per subgroup. Increasing the subgroup to \( n = 10 \) helps because
choices: the shift is measured in standard errors, which scale as \( 1/\sqrt n \)
larger subgroups are more likely to contain a bad part
quiz.solution: A shift of \( k \) process standard deviations is \( k\sqrt n \) standard errors, so \( n=10 \) turns a one-sigma shift from 2.24 to 3.16 standard errors and detection rises from 0.222 to 0.564. The false-alarm rate is unchanged at 0.0027 — three-sigma limits are three-sigma limits — and the cost is measuring twice as many parts per subgroup.

7.kuwait:
Applied case — the chart that was drawn with the wrong limits. A machining cell introduced control charts on a bore operation. The lines drawn on the chart were the drawing's own limits, 25.000 and 25.021 mm, because that was what everyone recognised. For eleven months no point ever came close to either line, the charts were filed, and the exercise was judged a success. Then a batch was rejected at assembly for bores that measured 25.024.

The chart had been incapable of signalling. Plotted on it were subgroup means of five, whose standard error is \( \sigma/\sqrt5 \); the correct control limits were \( \bar{\bar X}\pm A_2\bar R \), which for this process was \( \pm2.45\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) about a centre line of 10.2 µm — a band 4.9 µm wide inside a 21 µm specification. Every subgroup mean sat inside the specification because a mean of five is four times less variable than a part; that is arithmetic, not performance. Re-plotting the filed data against real control limits showed the level had shifted above the upper control limit five months earlier and stayed there.

Two practices follow. Control limits are computed from the process and nothing else — if the lines on a chart came off a drawing, the chart is decoration. And the fact that a chart never signals is not evidence of a good process; it is first evidence that the chart may not be able to signal. The check costs one calculation: limits that are not roughly \( \pm3\bar R/(d_2\sqrt n) \) about the process's own centre line are not control limits.
7.recap:
• Common-cause variation belongs to the process; special-cause variation is an assignable event. The two demand opposite responses, and telling them apart is the chart's only job.
  • Tampering — adjusting by the full deviation after every part — makes \( x_{n+1}=T-e_n+e_{n+1} \), doubling the variance and raising the standard deviation 41%.
  • A rational subgroup is chosen so that only common causes act within it, leaving special causes to show between subgroups.
  • \( \hat\sigma=\bar R/d_2 \) and the \( \bar X \) limits are \( \bar{\bar X}\pm A_2\bar R \) with \( A_2=3/(d_2\sqrt n) \) — three standard errors, packaged.
  • At \( n=5 \): \( d_2=2.326 \), \( A_2=0.577 \), \( D_4=2.114 \), \( D_3=0 \).
  • The worked chart gives limits 7.75 and 12.65 µm from \( \bar{\bar X}=10.2 \) and \( \bar R=4.25 \), with \( \hat\sigma=1.83\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and a range-chart limit of 8.98 µm.
  • Read the range chart first: the \( \bar X \) limits are computed from \( \bar R \). A mean-only signal means the level moved and the spread did not.
  • Control limits come from the process and apply to a subgroup statistic; specification limits come from the drawing and apply to a part. At \( n=5 \) they differ by a factor of \( \sqrt5 \) in scale, so mixing them makes a chart that cannot signal.
  • In control means predictable, not good: a stable process centred outside the tolerance produces scrap stably.
  • Three-sigma limits give a false alarm every 370 points, 6.5% over 25 points; a \( 1\sigma \) shift is caught in 4.5 subgroups at \( n=5 \) and a \( 2\sigma \) shift on the next one, with sensitivity scaling as \( \sqrt n \).

8.lecture:
§1 · When the data are counts, not measurements

Lesson 7's charts plot a measurement. Plenty of characteristics do not produce one — a part passes a limit gauge or it does not, a weld shows defects or it does not — and those need charts built on the distribution the counting itself follows.

Key relations — the attribute charts

\[ \bar p\pm3\sqrt{\frac{\bar p(1-\bar p)}{n}}\qquad\text{(fraction nonconforming, binomial)} \]

\[ \bar c\pm3\sqrt{\bar c}\qquad\text{(defects per unit, Poisson)} \]

The \( p \) chart counts nonconforming units out of \( n \); the \( c \) chart counts defects, of which one unit may carry several. Their limits are the three-sigma convention applied to the right distribution, not a new idea.

Take \( \bar p=0.03 \) with samples of 200. The standard error is \( \sqrt{0.03(0.97)/200}=0.01206 \), so the upper limit is \( 0.03+0.0362=0.0662 \) and the lower limit computes to \( -0.0062 \) — negative, so it is truncated to zero. That truncation is not a formality. It means the chart cannot detect an improvement: no sample, however clean, will ever fall below a limit of zero. The chart is one-sided by arithmetic.

Getting a usable lower limit means making \( \bar p>3\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)/n} \), which rearranges to \( n>9(1-\bar p)/\bar p \) — here \( 9(0.97)/0.03=291 \), so samples of 292 or more. At \( \bar p=0.003 \) it would be 2,991. This is the same point Lesson 5 made about limit gauges, in a new form: a pass/fail observation carries far less information than a measurement, so attribute charts need very large samples to say anything a variables chart says from five parts. Where a measurement is available, chart the measurement.

§2 · \( C_p \): could the process fit?

Stability, which Lesson 7 established, is not the same question as adequacy. A process can be perfectly stable and still too variable for the tolerance it has been given. The index that asks this is \( C_p \).

Key relation — potential capability

\[ C_p=\frac{\mathrm{USL}-\mathrm{LSL}}{6\hat\sigma},\qquad \hat\sigma=\frac{\bar R}{d_2} \]

A ratio of two widths: what is allowed, over what the process naturally produces. \( C_p=1 \) means the natural spread exactly fills the tolerance, which even perfectly centred leaves 0.27% outside — the same three-sigma tail as a control limit.

The bore process of Lesson 7 had \( \hat\sigma=1.83\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) against a 21 µm tolerance, so \( C_p=21/(6\times1.827)=1.92 \). Its spread occupies just over half the tolerance. Note carefully what has and has not been established by that number: \( C_p \) contains no information at all about where the process is sitting. It is a statement about the machine, not about the parts. For that reason it is sometimes called potential capability — what the process could achieve if someone centred it.

§3 · \( C_{pk} \): is it fitting?

The index that accounts for position takes the worse of the two sides.

Key relations — actual capability and the centring loss

\[ C_{pk}=\min\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{USL}-\mu}{3\hat\sigma},\ \frac{\mu-\mathrm{LSL}}{3\hat\sigma}\right),\qquad k=1-\frac{C_{pk}}{C_p} \]

\( C_{pk}\le C_p \) always, with equality only when the process is centred. The gap between them is pure centring: \( k \) is the fraction of the half-tolerance the mean has given away.

The diagram's process is the standard diagnostic case, and it answers the question directly. \( C_p=1.80 \) and \( C_{pk}=0.70 \) give \( k=1-0.70/1.80=0.611 \). Since \( C_p=1.80 \) means the tolerance is \( 10.8\hat\sigma \) wide, its half-width is \( 5.4\hat\sigma \), and the mean is \( 0.611\times5.4=3.3\hat\sigma \) off centre. Check it against the definition: the room remaining above is \( 5.4-3.3=2.1\hat\sigma \), and \( 2.1/3=0.70 \). The process is not too variable; it is badly aimed, and the fix is a setting, not a machine.

The defect rate follows from the near side alone. \( z=3C_{pk}=2.1 \), so the upper tail is \( 1-\Phi(2.1)=0.01786 \), about 17,900 parts per million. The lower tail sits \( 8.7\hat\sigma \) away and contributes nothing measurable. Every one of those 17,900 is recoverable by moving the mean.

Which answers the other standing question — what does \( C_{pk}=1.33 \) actually promise? \( z=3(1.33)=3.99 \), so the near tail is \( 1-\Phi(3.99)=3.30\times10^{-5} \): 33 parts per million on the near side. The familiar figure of 63 ppm is the two-sided total, and it is only correct if the process is centred, that is if \( C_p=C_{pk}=1.33 \). A process with \( C_p=3 \) and \( C_{pk}=1.33 \) has 33 ppm and nothing on the far side; a centred one has 33 on each. \( C_{pk} \) alone bounds the near tail and says nothing about the total, which is exactly why both indices are quoted together and neither is quoted alone.

The same arithmetic explains the most-quoted number in quality. A process with \( C_p=2 \) whose mean is allowed to wander \( 1.5\hat\sigma \) has \( C_{pk}=1.5 \), so \( z=4.5 \) and the tail is \( 3.40\times10^{-6} \) — 3.4 parts per million. The 1.5\( \sigma \) drift is a convention about long-term behaviour, not a law, and the 3.4 ppm is a consequence of assuming it.

§4 · Four ways a capability index lies

Capability indices are the most abused numbers in manufacturing, and every abuse is avoidable with one question each.

The process is not stable. \( \hat\sigma=\bar R/d_2 \) estimates the spread of a distribution, which presupposes there is one. On an out-of-control process the parameter being estimated changes while you estimate it, and the resulting index describes nothing. Stability first, capability second: that ordering is not a preference, it is a precondition, and computing \( C_{pk} \) before checking the charts is the single commonest error in the field.

The measuring system is inside the number. Independent variances add, so what a study observes is \( \sigma^2_{\text{obs}}=\sigma^2_{\text{process}}+\sigma^2_{\text{measurement}} \). A process at \( \sigma=1.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) measured with a gauge whose own spread is 1.0 µm reads \( \sqrt{1.5^2+1.0^2}=1.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), taking \( C_p \) from 2.33 to 1.94 — a 17% loss produced entirely by the instrument. How much of an observed spread belongs to the measuring system, and how to find out, is taken up later in this course.

The estimate is far softer than it looks. \( C_{pk} \) is computed from a sample and inherits its uncertainty. The standard large-sample interval is

Key relation — the confidence interval on \( C_{pk} \)

\[ \hat C_{pk}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{9n}+\frac{\hat C_{pk}^2}{2(n-1)}} \]

At \( \hat C_{pk}=1.33 \) from 30 parts the 95% interval is 0.97 to 1.69. From 100 parts it is 1.13 to 1.53. A single quoted index is a point estimate, and a small one is barely evidence.

A supplier reporting "\( C_{pk}=1.33 \), \( n=30 \)" has demonstrated that the true value is somewhere between not-capable and very capable. That is worth knowing before a study is accepted, and it is why capability studies specify a sample size rather than leaving it to whoever runs them.

The distribution is not normal. Every parts-per-million figure above comes from the normal tail. A skewed process — a form or position characteristic bounded at zero, a plated thickness — can show a respectable \( C_{pk} \) and a defect rate several times what the index implies, because the real tail is heavier than the model's. The index is still useful as a comparative measure; the ppm conversion is not.

Used properly, the study is a gate rather than a report. Before production starts, run the process, prove it is stable, then show the index clears the threshold the contract sets — commonly 1.33, and 1.67 where failure is expensive or unsafe. Doing it in that order is what makes capability a decision instead of an autopsy.

quiz.q:
Read a process from its two indices

Problem. A study reports \( C_p=1.80 \) and \( C_{pk}=0.70 \). Find the centring loss \( k \), how far the mean sits from the centre of the tolerance in process standard deviations, and the fraction of production outside the specification. Say what should be done, and what \( C_{pk} \) would become if it were done.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( k=1-C_{pk}/C_p=1-0.70/1.80=0.611 \).

(2) \( C_p=1.80 \) means the tolerance is \( 6(1.80)=10.8\hat\sigma \) wide, so its half-width is \( 5.4\hat\sigma \). The mean is displaced by \( k \) of that: \( 0.611\times5.4=3.3\hat\sigma \).

(3) Check against the definition: the room left on the near side is \( 5.4-3.3=2.1\hat\sigma \), and \( 2.1/3=0.70=C_{pk} \). Consistent.

(4) Near tail: \( z=3C_{pk}=2.1 \), so \( 1-\Phi(2.1)=0.01786 \). Far tail: \( z=5.4+3.3=8.7 \), which contributes about \( 10^{-18} \). Total 1.79%, or 17,900 ppm.

(5) The spread is fine and the aim is not, so the action is to move the mean to the centre of the tolerance — a setting change, not a machine problem. Centred, \( C_{pk}=C_p=1.80 \), and the defect rate falls to \( 2(1-\Phi(5.4))=6.7\times10^{-8} \), about 0.07 ppm.

Answer: \( k=0.611 \), the mean is \( 3.3\hat\sigma \) high, 1.79% (17,900 ppm) is outside; recentring alone takes \( C_{pk} \) to 1.80 and the defect rate to well under one ppm. Sanity check: the two indices together carry information neither has alone — \( C_p \) says the machine is capable, \( C_{pk} \) says the parts are not, and only the pair identifies centring as the cause. Note the leverage: a quarter of a million defective parts per fifteen million disappear for the cost of a tool offset, whereas improving \( C_p \) from 1.80 would have meant a new process. This is why a report quoting \( C_{pk} \) alone is incomplete.

quiz.q:
A capability study in inches, and how much to believe it

Problem. A shaft is specified 1.2490 / 1.2510 in. A stable process gives \( \mu=1.2504 \) in and \( \hat\sigma=0.00025 \) in. Find \( C_p \), both one-sided indices, \( C_{pk} \), and the defect rate in parts per million. Then, given that the study used 30 parts, give the 95% confidence interval on the reported \( C_{pk} \) and say what it means for an acceptance threshold of 1.33.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( C_p=(1.2510-1.2490)/(6\times0.00025)=0.0020/0.0015=1.333 \).

(2) Upper side: \( (1.2510-1.2504)/(3\times0.00025)=0.0006/0.00075=0.800 \).

(3) Lower side: \( (1.2504-1.2490)/0.00075=0.0014/0.00075=1.867 \).

(4) \( C_{pk}=\min(0.800,1.867)=0.800 \).

(5) Upper tail \( z=3(0.800)=2.4 \), giving \( 1-\Phi(2.4)=0.008198 \); lower tail \( z=5.6 \), giving \( 1.1\times10^{-8} \). Total 8,198 ppm, about 0.82%.

(6) With \( n=30 \) and \( \hat C_{pk}=0.800 \): \( \sqrt{1/(9\times30)+0.64/58}=\sqrt{0.003704+0.011034}=0.1214 \), so the interval is \( 0.800\pm1.96(0.1214)=0.562 \) to 1.038.

(7) The whole interval lies below 1.33, so the process fails the threshold and the sample size is not the reason — even the optimistic end of the interval is short.

Answer: \( C_p=1.333 \), \( C_{pu}=0.800 \), \( C_{pl}=1.867 \), \( C_{pk}=0.800 \), 8,198 ppm; the 95% interval is 0.56 to 1.04, entirely below the 1.33 gate. Sanity check: \( C_p \) and \( C_{pk} \) differ by a factor of 1.67, and the two one-sided indices show immediately why — the mean sits 0.0004 in above the centre of a 0.0020 in band, so 60% of the upper half-tolerance is gone. Note that the arithmetic never touched a unit conversion: the indices are ratios of lengths and are the same number in inches or millimetres. Note also what the interval does and does not settle — here it rules the process out, whereas a reported 1.33 from the same 30 parts would have ranged from 0.97 to 1.69 and settled nothing.

quiz.q:
Two things that are not the process

Problem. A tolerance of 21 µm is checked on a process whose true standard deviation is 1.5 µm, using a gauge whose own measurement standard deviation is 1.0 µm. Find the observed \( C_p \), the true \( C_p \), and the fraction of the index lost to the instrument. Separately, a \( p \) chart runs at \( \bar p=0.03 \) with samples of 200: give its limits and state what the chart cannot do, and find the smallest sample size that fixes it.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Independent variances add: \( \sigma_{\text{obs}}=\sqrt{1.5^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt{3.25}=1.803\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) \( C_{p,\text{obs}}=21/(6\times1.803)=1.941 \).

(3) \( C_{p,\text{true}}=21/(6\times1.5)=2.333 \).

(4) Loss \( =1-1.941/2.333=0.168 \), so 17% of the index was consumed by the measuring system, not by the process.

(5) \( p \) chart: \( \sqrt{0.03(0.97)/200}=0.01206 \), so \( \mathrm{UCL}=0.03+0.0362=0.0662 \) and the lower limit computes to \( -0.0062 \), which is truncated to 0.

(6) With a lower limit of zero no sample can ever fall below it, so the chart cannot detect an improvement — only a deterioration.

(7) A positive lower limit needs \( \bar p>3\sqrt{\bar p(1-\bar p)/n} \), that is \( n>9(1-\bar p)/\bar p=9(0.97)/0.03=291 \). Samples of 292 or more.

Answer: observed \( C_p=1.94 \) against a true 2.33, a 17% loss to the gauge; the \( p \) chart runs 0 to 0.0662 and is blind to improvement below \( n=292 \). Sanity check: both results are the same lesson in different clothing — the number a study reports is a property of the measurement scheme as well as of the process. The gauge cost more index than most process improvements would have gained, and the \( p \) chart's blindness is arithmetic rather than bad luck. Note that a variables chart on the same characteristic would have signalled from five parts, which is the argument for measuring wherever a measurement exists.

quiz.solution: Independent variances add: \( \sqrt{1.5^2+1.0^2}=\sqrt{3.25}=1.80\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). 8.kuwait:
Applied case — the capability study that was run on the wrong week. A supplier had to demonstrate \( C_{pk}\ge1.33 \) on a bore before a production order was released. The study was run on 30 consecutive parts from a single setup, returned \( C_{pk}=1.38 \), and the order was placed. Rejects in the first production month ran near 2%.

Three things had gone wrong, and each was checkable in advance. No control chart accompanied the study, so nobody had shown the process was stable; 30 consecutive parts from one setup capture the variation within a setup and almost none of the variation between setups, which is where this process moved. The sample size made the number soft in any case: at \( \hat C_{pk}=1.38 \) with \( n=30 \) the 95% interval runs from about 1.01 to 1.75, so 1.38 was never evidence of clearing 1.33. And the gauge's own variation sat inside \( \hat\sigma \) unexamined, which if anything made the reported figure conservative — the one error that happened to work in the supplier's favour and still told nobody anything true.

Two practices follow. A capability study is not a number, it is a number plus the conditions that produced it: the control charts showing stability, the sampling plan showing what sources of variation were allowed to act, the sample size, and the state of the measuring system. And an acceptance threshold should be applied to the lower confidence limit rather than to the point estimate, which is what turns "we measured 1.38" into "we have demonstrated 1.33".

  • \( C_{pk} \) takes the worse side, so \( C_{pk}\le C_p \) always, and \( k=1-C_{pk}/C_p \) is the fraction of the half-tolerance lost to aim.
  • \( C_p=1.80 \) with \( C_{pk}=0.70 \) means \( k=0.611 \), a mean \( 3.3\hat\sigma \) off centre, and 17,900 ppm outside — all of it recoverable by moving the mean.
  • \( C_{pk}=1.33 \) promises 33 ppm on the near side; the familiar 63 ppm is the two-sided total and holds only if the process is centred.
  • The 3.4 ppm figure is \( C_p=2 \) with an assumed \( 1.5\hat\sigma \) drift, so \( C_{pk}=1.5 \) and \( z=4.5 \) — a convention, not a law.
  • Stability first, capability second: \( \hat\sigma \) estimates a distribution, which an out-of-control process does not have.
  • The gauge is inside the index: \( \sigma^2_{\rm obs}=\sigma^2_{\rm proc}+\sigma^2_{\rm meas} \), and a 1.0 µm gauge on a 1.5 µm process costs 17% of \( C_p \).
