9.lecture:
§1 · The plan, and the curve that is the plan

A lot arrives. Inspecting all of it may be impossible, uneconomic, or destructive, so a single sampling plan takes \( n \) parts at random and accepts the lot if the number of defectives \( d \) is at most the acceptance number \( c \). Two integers, and the whole behaviour of the scheme follows from them.

Key relation — the operating-characteristic curve

\[ P_a(p)=\sum_{d=0}^{c}\binom{n}{d}p^{\,d}(1-p)^{\,n-d} \]

The probability of accepting a lot whose true fraction defective is \( p \). Plotted against \( p \) this is the OC curve, and it is a complete description of the plan — every other property quoted about a plan is a point read off it.

For \( n=125 \), \( c=3 \): a lot at 1% defective is accepted 96.3% of the time, at 2% it is accepted 75.9%, at 3% 48.1%, and at 5% 12.4%. Notice what the curve is not. It is not a step. There is no fraction defective below which acceptance is certain and above which rejection is certain, because the plan sees only a sample and a sample is a random draw. Every plan that inspects fewer than all the parts has a sloping curve, and every sloping curve means both parties carry a risk.

§2 · The two risks, which are the two errors of a test

Those risks have names, and they are the familiar pair from hypothesis testing wearing work clothes.

Key definitions — the two risks

\[ \alpha=1-P_a(\mathrm{AQL})\quad\text{(producer's risk)},\qquad \beta=P_a(\mathrm{LTPD})\quad\text{(consumer's risk)} \]

\( \alpha \) is the chance a good lot is rejected — a type I error, and the supplier pays for it. \( \beta \) is the chance a bad lot is accepted — a type II error, and the customer pays for it. Conventionally \( \alpha=0.05 \) and \( \beta=0.10 \).

Reading the reference plan's curve at those two probabilities gives its two defining qualities. It accepts 95% of lots at \( p=1.10\% \), so 1.10% is the acceptable quality level for this plan; and it accepts 10% of lots at \( p=5.27\% \), so 5.27% is the lot tolerance percent defective. The ratio of the two, \( 5.27/1.10=4.79 \), is the plan's discrimination ratio — how much worse a lot has to be before the plan reliably notices.

Only one thing improves that ratio, and it is not the acceptance number. Compare four plans, each chosen to hold roughly the same AQL: \( n=50,c=1 \) discriminates at 10.56; \( n=125,c=3 \) at 4.79; \( n=200,c=5 \) at 3.49; \( n=500,c=12 \) at 2.29. Sample size buys discrimination, and nothing else does.

Which disposes of the most durable piece of folklore in the subject: that a sample should be some percentage of the lot. It should not, because the OC curve barely depends on lot size at all. Taking 125 parts from a lot of 1,000 that is 3% defective accepts it with probability 0.4713; taking the same 125 from a lot of 100,000 at the same 3% accepts with probability 0.4813. The lot grew a hundredfold and the plan's behaviour moved by one point in a hundred. A plan is defined by \( n \) and \( c \); "10% of the lot" is a rule that inspects far too many small lots and far too few large ones.

§3 · What an AQL does not mean

The AQL is the most misread number in quality, in two distinct ways, and both are worth stating as flat corrections.

It is not a target, and it is not permission. The AQL is a property of the plan — the quality it happens to accept 95% of the time. It is not an agreement that the supplier may run at that level. A supplier who does run at exactly the AQL will have one lot in twenty rejected, and across twenty consecutive lots the chance of at least one rejection is \( 1-0.95^{20}=64\% \). Sitting on the AQL is not a comfortable place to be; it is the edge of the plan's tolerance for you.

An accepted lot is not a good lot. Acceptance is a decision about the lot, not a certificate about its parts. A lot accepted at \( p=3\% \) still contains 3% defectives, all of which proceed into assembly. Sampling never removes defectives from an accepted lot; it only decides whether the lot goes forward.

What sampling can bound is the long-run average, provided rejected lots are screened rather than returned unchanged.

Key relation — average outgoing quality

\[ \mathrm{AOQ}(p)\approx p\,P_a(p),\qquad \mathrm{AOQL}=\max_p\ \mathrm{AOQ}(p) \]

Accepted lots pass at \( p \); rejected lots are 100%-inspected and their defectives replaced, so they pass at nearly zero. The product has a maximum — incoming quality that is very good produces little outgoing defect, and incoming quality that is very bad is almost always rejected and rectified.

For the reference plan the maximum is \( \mathrm{AOQL}=1.55\% \), occurring at an incoming level of 2.34%. That is a genuine guarantee with a genuine condition: however bad the supplier's process becomes, long-run outgoing quality cannot exceed 1.55% defective — if every rejected lot is really screened and rectified. Where rejected lots are returned to the supplier and shipped back untouched, the AOQL is not a bound on anything.

§4 · When to sample, and when 100% inspection is owed

The economic answer is sharper than most people expect, and it says that sampling is usually the wrong choice.

Key relation — the all-or-none rule

\[ p^{*}=\frac{k_1}{k_2}:\qquad pp^{*}\Rightarrow\text{inspect all} \]

\( k_1 \) is the cost of inspecting one part and \( k_2 \) the cost of one defective passing into production. For a stable process at known \( p \), the minimum-cost policy is one of the two extremes; partial sampling costs more than the better of them.

With inspection at 0.40 per part and an escape costing 55, the break-even is \( p^{*}=0.40/55=0.73\% \). A process running at 0.2% defective costs \( 0.002\times55=0.11 \) per part if nothing is inspected, against 0.40 per part to screen: inspect nothing. The same process drifted to 2% costs \( 1.10 \) per part unscreened: inspect everything. There is no value of \( p \) at which checking one part in eight is the cheapest policy.

So why does acceptance sampling exist at all? Because the rule's premise — a stable process at known \( p \) — is exactly what a receiving inspector does not have. Lots arrive from a supplier whose process state is invisible, may be stable or not, and may differ lot to lot. Sampling is the rational hedge under that ignorance, and it is also a contractual instrument: it gives both sides a defined, auditable rule. Its right home is incoming inspection from an unverified source, and its natural replacement is evidence — a supplier who can produce control charts and capability studies has told you \( p \), and once \( p \) is known the all-or-none rule applies.

Three situations override the arithmetic entirely. Where the test is destructive, sampling is not a choice but the only possibility, and the plan's discrimination has to be paid for in scrapped parts. Where the consequence of an escape is a safety event, no escape rate is acceptable and the answer is 100% inspection with redundancy, or a design that removes the failure mode. And where the process is not in control, \( p \) is not a number, so no policy derived from it is valid until stability is restored.

One honest qualification belongs with all of this. "100% inspection" is a name, not a guarantee: attribute inspection typically detects 80–95% of the defectives present, so a 2% incoming rate screened at 90% efficiency still passes 0.2%. A second pass takes it to 0.02% and a third to 0.002%, which is why critical characteristics get redundant checks rather than one careful one. The instrument, the inspector and the plan are all part of the same measuring system, and none of them is perfect.

quiz.q:
Read a plan off its own curve

Problem. A single sampling plan takes \( n=125 \) and accepts on \( c=3 \). Give the probability of accepting lots at 1%, 3% and 5% defective. The plan's AQL (the quality accepted 95% of the time) is 1.10% and its LTPD (accepted 10% of the time) is 5.27%; state the producer's and consumer's risks and the discrimination ratio. Then find the probability that a supplier running at exactly the AQL has at least one of twenty consecutive lots rejected.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( P_a(p)=\sum_{d=0}^{3}\binom{125}{d}p^d(1-p)^{125-d} \).

(2) At \( p=0.01 \): the four terms are 0.2847, 0.3595, 0.2251 and 0.0932, giving \( P_a=0.963 \).

(3) At \( p=0.03 \): \( P_a=0.481 \). At \( p=0.05 \): \( P_a=0.124 \).

(4) Producer's risk \( \alpha=1-P_a(\mathrm{AQL})=1-0.95=0.05 \): one good lot in twenty is rejected. Consumer's risk \( \beta=P_a(\mathrm{LTPD})=0.10 \): one lot in ten at 5.27% defective is accepted and shipped.

(5) Discrimination ratio \( =5.27/1.10=4.79 \). A lot must be nearly five times worse than the AQL before the plan rejects it reliably.

(6) Lots are independent, so \( P=1-0.95^{20}=1-0.3585=0.642 \).

Answer: \( P_a \) = 0.963, 0.481, 0.124 at 1%, 3% and 5%; \( \alpha=0.05 \), \( \beta=0.10 \), discrimination ratio 4.79; a supplier at the AQL has a 64% chance of at least one rejection in twenty lots. Sanity check: the curve falls from 0.96 to 0.12 as \( p \) goes from 1% to 5%, which is gradual, not a step — and that gradualness is the two risks. Note what the 64% means in practice: the AQL is not a safe operating point for a supplier, and treating it as a target guarantees regular arguments over rejected lots that were exactly as agreed. The place to sit is well below the AQL, which is the same conclusion the capability threshold of Lesson 8 reaches from the other direction.

quiz.q:
Two pieces of folklore, tested

Problem. (a) A quality manual requires the sample to be "10% of the lot". Taking \( n=125 \), \( c=3 \) from lots that are 3% defective, the exact acceptance probabilities are 0.4713 for a lot of 1,000 and 0.4813 for a lot of 100,000. Comment on what this implies for the 10% rule. (b) The same plan is used with rejected lots 100%-inspected and rectified. Given that \( \mathrm{AOQ}(p)\approx pP_a(p) \) peaks at 1.55% when \( p=2.34\% \), state what is and is not guaranteed, and evaluate \( \mathrm{AOQ} \) at \( p=1\% \) and \( p=6\% \) using \( P_a=0.9626 \) and \( P_a=0.0539 \).
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The lot grew by a factor of 100 and \( P_a \) moved from 0.4713 to 0.4813 — one part in a hundred. The plan's behaviour is governed by \( n \) and \( c \), not by the fraction of the lot they represent.

(2) So the 10% rule inspects 100 parts from a lot of 1,000 — roughly the right sample — and 10,000 from a lot of 100,000, which buys discrimination nobody asked for at eighty times the cost. Run the other way, on a lot of 200 it takes 20 parts, a plan far too weak to discriminate at all. The rule is wrong in both directions.

(3) \( \mathrm{AOQ}(0.01)=0.01\times0.9626=0.96\% \). Most lots pass, carrying their defectives with them.

(4) \( \mathrm{AOQ}(0.06)=0.06\times0.0539=0.32\% \). Incoming quality is far worse, but almost every lot is rejected and rectified, so little defect gets through.

(5) Between those extremes lies the maximum, 1.55% at \( p=2.34\% \). What is guaranteed is that long-run average outgoing quality cannot exceed 1.55% defective whatever the supplier does. What is not guaranteed is anything about a particular lot: an accepted lot at 3% still contains 3% defectives. And the guarantee fails entirely if rejected lots are returned unscreened rather than rectified.

Answer: (a) lot size is nearly irrelevant, so the 10% rule over-inspects large lots and under-inspects small ones; (b) AOQ is 0.96% at \( p=1\% \) and 0.32% at \( p=6\% \), with a guaranteed long-run ceiling of 1.55% that depends entirely on rejected lots actually being screened. Sanity check: AOQ falling at both ends is the right shape — good incoming quality produces few defectives and bad incoming quality gets rejected — so a maximum in between must exist. Note the two conditions that are easy to lose: the ceiling is a long-run average and not a property of any lot, and it evaporates the moment rejected lots go back to the supplier and return untouched.

quiz.q:
Sample, screen, or leave it alone (with a per-gross cost)

Problem. Inspecting one part costs 0.40 and one defective escaping into production costs 55, in the same units. For a stable process, find the break-even fraction defective and give the minimum-cost policy at \( p=0.2\% \) and at \( p=2\% \). Then repeat the break-even calculation for a fastener line where inspection is quoted at 48 per gross. Finally, if 100% inspection detects 90% of the defectives present, find the outgoing rate from a 2% incoming rate after one, two and three passes.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Cost per part of inspecting nothing is \( pk_2 \); of inspecting everything, \( k_1 \). They are equal at \( p^{*}=k_1/k_2=0.40/55=0.00727 \), that is 0.73%.

(2) At \( p=0.002 \): unscreened costs \( 0.002\times55=0.11 \) per part, screening costs 0.40. Inspect nothing.

(3) At \( p=0.02 \): unscreened costs \( 0.02\times55=1.10 \) per part against 0.40. Inspect everything. No intermediate sampling fraction beats the better extreme, because both costs are linear in the fraction inspected.

(4) A gross is 144 parts, so \( k_1=48/144=0.3333 \) per part and \( p^{*}=0.3333/55=0.00606 \), that is 0.61% — 6,061 parts per million.

(5) Each pass leaves 10% of what it was given: \( 0.02(0.10)=0.2\% \), then \( 0.02\%\), then \( 0.002\% \).

Answer: \( p^{*}=0.73\% \); inspect nothing at 0.2% and everything at 2%; at 48 per gross the break-even is 0.61%; screening at 90% efficiency gives 0.2%, 0.02% and 0.002% after one, two and three passes. Sanity check: the rule assumes a stable process at a known \( p \), which is exactly what a receiving inspector lacks — and that, rather than economics, is why acceptance sampling exists. Note that the per-gross figure needed only a count conversion, and the answer moved from 0.73% to 0.61% because inspection got cheaper, which is the direction it should move. Note finally that "100% inspection" is a name: one pass at 90% still ships 2,000 defectives per million, which is why critical characteristics are checked redundantly rather than carefully.

the chance a good lot is rejected
the fraction defective the supplier is allowed

wrong, because a plan's discrimination depends on \( n \) and \( c \) rather than on the fraction of the lot sampled

the supplier's process is in control

9.kuwait:
Applied case — the AQL that was read as an allowance. A purchase specification for machined fittings called for inspection at "AQL 1.0". The supplier's quality plan set the process aim so that about 1% of parts were nonconforming, on the stated reasoning that 1% was what the contract allowed. Lots were rejected repeatedly, each rejection was disputed, and both sides believed the other was in breach.

Both readings of the number were wrong in the same way. An AQL is a property of the sampling plan — the quality it accepts about 95% of the time — not a permitted defect rate. A supplier sitting exactly on it faces \( 1-0.95^{20}=64\% \) odds of at least one rejection in twenty lots, so the rejections were the plan working as designed, not evidence of a worse process than agreed. The customer's position was no better founded: accepted lots at 1% defective had been carrying 1% defectives into assembly the whole time, because acceptance is a decision about a lot and never a treatment of it.

Two practices follow. Write the specification in terms both sides can check — the plan \( (n,c) \), the resulting AQL and LTPD, and the risks each party is accepting — rather than a bare AQL figure that invites the allowance reading. And prefer evidence to sampling where it can be had: a supplier who supplies control charts and capability studies has stated the process fraction defective directly, at which point the receiving decision stops being a gamble on a sample and becomes the straightforward cost comparison of the all-or-none rule.

  • Lot size barely matters — 125 parts from a 3% lot of 1,000 accepts at 0.4713, from 100,000 at 0.4813 — so "10% of the lot" is wrong in both directions.
  • An AQL is a property of the plan, not a target: a supplier sitting on it has a 64% chance of at least one rejection in twenty lots.
  • An accepted lot is not a good lot; sampling removes nothing from it.
  • \( \mathrm{AOQ}=pP_a(p) \) peaks at \( \mathrm{AOQL}=1.55\% \) when \( p=2.34\% \), and that ceiling holds only if rejected lots are genuinely screened and rectified.

10.lecture:
§1 · The measuring system has a variance of its own

Lesson 8 made the point in passing and then moved on: what a study observes is not the process. Every reading is the part plus the measurement, and because those two are independent their variances add.

Key relation — the observed variance

\[ \sigma^2_{\text{obs}}=\sigma^2_{\text{part}}+\sigma^2_{\text{gauge}},\qquad \sigma^2_{\text{gauge}}=\sigma^2_{\text{EV}}+\sigma^2_{\text{AV}} \]

Repeatability (equipment variation, EV) is the scatter of one operator measuring one part with one gauge, repeatedly — the instrument and the method talking. Reproducibility (appraiser variation, AV) is the scatter between operators measuring the same parts — the people, or more often the procedure they were given.

Everything else in this lesson is bookkeeping on those two terms. The reason it matters is that every number in the previous three lessons was computed from measured data: the control limits of Lesson 7, the \( \hat\sigma \) behind Lesson 8's indices, and the accept/reject decision on every part. If the measuring system's share of the variance is unknown, so is the meaning of all of them.

The distinction between the two components is diagnostic, not academic. High repeatability variation points at the gauge, the fixture, the location the part is held in, or a method that leaves the reading to judgement. High reproducibility variation points at the instructions — two operators doing genuinely different things, both convinced they are following the procedure. They have different cures, and a single combined figure tells you which to buy nothing about.

§2 · The crossed study, using the estimator you already have

The standard design is crossed: every operator measures every part, several times. Ten parts, three operators, three trials is 90 readings and is the usual size. The parts must span the real process range — a study run on ten parts hand-picked from the middle of the distribution will report a gauge far worse than it is, because it has shrunk the part variation it is compared against.

The arithmetic needs no new machinery. Ranges convert to standard deviations exactly as in Lesson 7.

Key relations — the average-and-range method

\[ \sigma_{\text{EV}}=\frac{\bar R}{d_2},\qquad \sigma_{\text{AV}}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{R_o}{d_2}\right)^{2}-\frac{\sigma^2_{\text{EV}}}{n\,r}},\qquad \sigma_{\text{PV}}=\frac{R_p}{d_2} \]

\( \bar R \) is the mean of the within-cell ranges, \( R_o \) the range of the operator averages, \( R_p \) the range of the part averages, with \( d_2 \) taken at the relevant count — 1.693 for three, 3.078 for ten. The subtraction in \( \sigma_{\text{AV}} \) is essential: an operator's average already carries repeatability error, \( \sigma^2_{\text{EV}}/nr \) of it, and leaving it in would charge the operators for the gauge.

A study on a bore gives \( \bar R=5.4\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), \( R_o=4.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and \( R_p=34\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), with \( n=10 \), \( r=3 \), against a 100 µm tolerance. Then \( \sigma_{\text{EV}}=5.4/1.693=3.19\ \mu\mathrm{m} \); \( (4.5/1.693)^2=7.065 \) less \( 3.19^2/30=0.339 \) gives \( \sigma_{\text{AV}}=2.59\ \mu\mathrm{m} \); so \( \mathrm{GRR}=\sqrt{3.19^2+2.59^2}=4.11\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The parts give \( \mathrm{PV}=34/3.078=11.05\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), and \( \mathrm{TV}=\sqrt{4.11^2+11.05^2}=11.79\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

One honest note on the constants. Using \( d_2 \) throughout is the usual teaching form and is right for \( \bar R \), which averages thirty cell ranges. A single range of three operator averages is a one-subgroup estimate, for which standards tabulate a slightly different small-sample constant; the difference is a few per cent and changes no verdict here. The modern alternative is to run the study as an analysis of variance, which estimates the same components directly and additionally detects operator-by-part interaction that the range method cannot see.

§3 · The verdict, and what 35% actually costs

Two ratios are reported, and they answer different questions.

Key relations — the two verdicts and the resolution

\[ \%\mathrm{GRR}_{\text{process}}=100\frac{\mathrm{GRR}}{\mathrm{TV}},\qquad \%\mathrm{GRR}_{\text{tolerance}}=100\frac{6\,\mathrm{GRR}}{\mathrm{USL}-\mathrm{LSL}},\qquad \mathrm{ndc}=\left\lfloor\sqrt2\,\frac{\mathrm{PV}}{\mathrm{GRR}}\right\rfloor \]

The first asks whether the gauge can see the process — the question that matters for control charts and capability. The second asks whether it can see the tolerance — the question that matters for accepting parts. Under 10% is accepted, over 30% is not, and 10–30% is judged on what the gauge is for. \( \mathrm{ndc} \) is the number of distinct categories the gauge can resolve across the part spread.

For this study \( \%\mathrm{GRR}_{\text{process}}=100(4.11/11.79)=34.9\% \), and \( \%\mathrm{GRR}_{\text{tolerance}}=100(6\times4.11)/100=24.7\% \). The two verdicts differ, and both are correct: this gauge is unacceptable for process control and marginal for conformance decisions. A single number would have hidden that.

Now the part that surprises people, and it is worth doing carefully because the intuition is wrong. Thirty-five per cent sounds like a third of the data is noise. In variance it is \( 4.11^2/11.79^2=12.2\% \), and the effect on the process standard deviation is smaller still: removing the gauge entirely would take \( \sigma \) from 11.79 to 11.05, a fall of 6.7%, and lift \( C_p \) from 1.41 to 1.51. Quadrature is forgiving that way — which is exactly why \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) is a poor guide to how much the gauge is distorting a capability index.

What 35% destroys is resolution. \( \mathrm{ndc}=\lfloor1.41\times11.05/4.11\rfloor=3 \): the gauge sorts this process into three categories, which is barely more than pass, middle and fail. The constant is \( \sqrt2 \), and the meaning is the number of non-overlapping intervals of gauge uncertainty that fit inside the part spread. Five is the usual minimum for a variables control chart; below that the chart is plotting the gauge. The concrete cost on an \( \bar X \) chart is that the limits, computed from inflated data, are too wide: a genuine one-standard-deviation shift in the process is detected with probability 0.183 instead of 0.222, so the average run length to catch it goes from 4.5 subgroups to 5.5 — 22% slower, permanently, from an instrument nobody is looking at.

§4 · What to do about it

Start by reading which component is large, because the two have different prices.

Here \( \sigma^2_{\text{EV}}=10.17 \) and \( \sigma^2_{\text{AV}}=6.73 \), so 60% of the gauge's variance is repeatability — equipment and method, not people. Training the operators would address the smaller share. What addresses the larger share is a better fixture, a more definite location for the part, a finer instrument, or simply averaging: the mean of \( r \) readings has repeatability variance \( \sigma^2_{\text{EV}}/r \). Averaging three readings takes \( \sigma_{\text{EV}} \) from 3.19 to 1.84, \( \mathrm{GRR} \) to 3.18, \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) to 27.7% and \( \mathrm{ndc} \) to 4 — a real improvement bought with time rather than capital. Had \( \sigma_{\text{AV}} \) dominated instead, none of that would have helped and the answer would have been the work instruction.

Resolution belongs in the same audit. A rounded reading contributes a variance of \( (\text{resolution})^2/12 \), so a 1 µm instrument adds 0.29 µm and is negligible here, while a 5 µm instrument would add 1.44 µm — a fifth of the repeatability, from the display alone. The old rule of thumb that the discrimination should be a tenth of the process spread or the tolerance is this calculation in disguise.

Meanwhile, parts still have to be accepted or rejected with the gauge you have, and the honest way to do that is the guard band of Lesson 3 — the same rule, with the study's \( \sigma_{\text{GRR}} \) in place of a certificate's expanded uncertainty, because the repeatability and reproducibility measured here are the working-condition version of the same quantity.

Key relation — guard banding

\[ \text{accept only if } |y|\le \frac{T}{2}-z_{\gamma}\,\sigma_{\text{GRR}} \]

Pulling the acceptance limit inside the specification by \( z_\gamma \) gauge standard deviations makes a false acceptance at that confidence impossible. It buys that confidence with tolerance, and the price is set entirely by the gauge.

At 95% one-sided confidence, \( z=1.645 \), so the band is \( 1.645\times4.11=6.76\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at each end — 13.5% of the 100 µm tolerance surrendered to the measuring system. With a 1.0 µm gauge the same confidence would cost 3.3%. That is the number to put in front of whoever is deciding whether a better instrument is worth buying, because it is denominated in the thing the shop actually values.

Two ordering rules close the subject. The study comes before the control charts and the capability study, not after them, because both are computed from measured data and a study run afterwards can only invalidate work already done. And the parts used must span the real process range: a study on ten similar parts understates \( \mathrm{PV} \), inflates \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \), and condemns a gauge that was adequate — the mirror image of the error it is meant to catch.

quiz.q:
Work a crossed study end to end

Problem. A crossed study uses 10 parts, 3 operators and 3 trials. The mean of the within-cell ranges is \( \bar R=5.4\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), the range of the three operator averages is \( R_o=4.5\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), and the range of the ten part averages is \( R_p=34\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Take \( d_2=1.693 \) for three and 3.078 for ten. Find EV, AV, GRR, PV and TV, then \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) against both the process and a 100 µm tolerance, and the number of distinct categories. Give the verdict.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( \sigma_{\text{EV}}=\bar R/d_2=5.4/1.693=3.19\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) The operator spread is \( R_o/d_2=4.5/1.693=2.658 \), but an operator's average already carries repeatability error worth \( \sigma^2_{\text{EV}}/nr=10.17/30=0.339 \). So \( \sigma^2_{\text{AV}}=2.658^2-0.339=7.065-0.339=6.726 \) and \( \sigma_{\text{AV}}=2.59\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(3) \( \mathrm{GRR}=\sqrt{3.19^2+2.59^2}=\sqrt{10.17+6.73}=\sqrt{16.90} =4.11\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(4) \( \mathrm{PV}=34/3.078=11.05\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so \( \mathrm{TV}=\sqrt{16.90+122.02}=\sqrt{138.92}=11.79\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(5) \( \%\mathrm{GRR}_{\text{process}}=100(4.11/11.79)=34.9\% \).

(6) \( \%\mathrm{GRR}_{\text{tolerance}}=100(6\times4.11)/100=24.7\% \).

(7) \( \mathrm{ndc}=\lfloor1.41\times11.05/4.11\rfloor=\lfloor3.79\rfloor=3 \).

(8) Over 30% against the process: unacceptable for process control. Between 10 and 30% against the tolerance: marginal for accept/reject, to be judged on the cost of an error.

Answer: EV 3.19, AV 2.59, GRR 4.11, PV 11.05, TV 11.79 µm; \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) 34.9% to the process and 24.7% to the tolerance; ndc = 3. Unacceptable for charting, marginal for conformance. Sanity check: the two verdicts differ because they answer different questions, and reporting only one of them is how a gauge gets approved for the wrong job. Note the subtraction in step 2: it is worth 0.339 of variance here, small, but omitting it charges the operators for the equipment and misdirects the fix. Note finally that ndc = 3 is the binding result — a control chart drawn with a gauge that resolves three categories is largely plotting the instrument.

quiz.q:
What 35% costs, and what it does not

Problem. For the study above (GRR 4.11, PV 11.05, TV 11.79 µm, tolerance 100 µm), find the gauge's share of the variance, the percentage by which the observed standard deviation is inflated, and \( C_p \) computed with and without the gauge. Then find the probability that an \( \bar X \) chart with \( n=5 \) detects a one-standard-deviation process shift using this gauge, against a perfect one, and the average run lengths.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Variance share: \( \mathrm{GRR}^2/\mathrm{TV}^2=16.90/138.92=12.2\% \) — not 34.9%, because the ratio of standard deviations is not the ratio of variances.

(2) Inflation of the standard deviation: \( \mathrm{TV}/\mathrm{PV}=11.79/11.05=1.067 \), so 6.7%.

(3) \( C_p \) with the gauge: \( 100/(6\times11.79)=1.41 \). Without it: \( 100/(6\times11.05)=1.51 \). The index is 6.3% low.

(4) A shift of one true process standard deviation is \( 11.05/11.79=0.937 \) observed standard deviations, so on the chart it is \( 0.937\sqrt5=2.096 \) standard errors instead of \( \sqrt5=2.236 \).

(5) Detection: \( 1-\Phi(3-2.096)=1-\Phi(0.904)=0.183 \), against \( 1-\Phi(0.764)=0.222 \) with a perfect gauge.

(6) Average run lengths: \( 1/0.183=5.47 \) subgroups against \( 1/0.222=4.50 \) — 22% slower.

Answer: the gauge is 12.2% of the variance and inflates \( \sigma \) by 6.7%, costing 6.3% of \( C_p \); detection of a \( 1\sigma \) shift falls from 0.222 to 0.183 and the run length rises from 4.50 to 5.47 subgroups. Sanity check: a figure that reads as "a third of my data is noise" turns out to cost 6% of a capability index, which is the quadrature at work and worth internalising before arguing for a new instrument on the strength of \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) alone. The real damage is elsewhere: ndc = 3 and a chart that is permanently 22% slower to notice a shift. Note that the penalty is invisible in the data — the chart looks normal, the limits look reasonable, and they are simply too wide.

quiz.q:
Guard bands and fixes, in two unit systems

Problem. With \( \mathrm{GRR}=4.11\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) and a 100 µm tolerance, find the guard band needed for 95% one-sided confidence that an accepted part really conforms, and express it as a percentage of the tolerance; repeat for a gauge at \( \mathrm{GRR}=1.0\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). Then, given \( \sigma_{\text{EV}}=3.19 \) and \( \sigma_{\text{AV}}=2.59\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), say which fix is worth buying and find \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) if each measurement becomes the mean of three readings (PV stays 11.05). Finally repeat the guard-band calculation for a gauge at \( \mathrm{GRR}=0.00016 \) in against a 0.0040 in tolerance.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) For 95% one-sided confidence, \( z=1.645 \), so the band is \( 1.645\times4.11=6.76\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at each end.

(2) Both ends: \( 13.52\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) of a 100 µm tolerance, that is 13.5% surrendered to the measuring system.

(3) At \( \mathrm{GRR}=1.0 \): \( 2\times1.645=3.29\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), or 3.3%. The difference, 10 percentage points of tolerance, is what the better instrument buys.

(4) \( \sigma^2_{\text{EV}}=10.17 \) against \( \sigma^2_{\text{AV}}=6.73 \), so 60% of the gauge's variance is repeatability — equipment, fixture and method, not the operators. Training addresses the smaller share.

(5) Averaging three readings divides the repeatability variance by three: \( \sigma_{\text{EV}}=3.19/\sqrt3=1.84 \), so \( \mathrm{GRR}=\sqrt{3.39+6.73}=3.18 \), \( \mathrm{TV}=\sqrt{10.12+122.02}=11.49 \), and \( \%\mathrm{GRR}=100(3.18/11.49)=27.7\% \), with ndc rising to 4.

(6) In inches: \( 1.645\times0.00016=0.000263 \) in each side, \( 0.000527 \) in total, which is \( 13.2\% \) of 0.0040 in. (The gauge is \( 0.00016\times25400=4.06\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), so the same answer in different clothes.)

Answer: 6.76 µm each side, 13.5% of tolerance, falling to 3.3% with a 1.0 µm gauge; repeatability dominates, so averaging three readings is the cheap fix and takes \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) to 27.7% with ndc 4; the inch case gives 0.000263 in each side, 13.2%. Sanity check: the guard band is the right currency for this argument — a shop that shrugs at "34.9% GRR" will not shrug at losing 13.5% of its tolerance, and the two statements are the same fact. Note that averaging helps only because EV dominates here; if the operators had been the larger term, three readings each would have bought almost nothing and the answer would have been to rewrite the method. Note also that the inch and micrometre cases agree once converted, as they must — the guard band is a length, not an index.

quiz.q: Repeatability and reproducibility are, respectively, the variation
choices: between operators, and within one operator
within one operator and gauge on one part, and between operators
of the parts, and of the gauge
quiz.solution: Repeatability is one operator, one part, one gauge, repeated — the equipment and the method talking. Reproducibility is the scatter between operators on the same parts, which in practice usually means the work instruction rather than the people. The two have different cures, which is why a combined figure alone tells you nothing about what to fix.

quiz.q: A study returns \( \%\mathrm{GRR}=35\% \) against the process variation. For an SPC deployment this means
choices: the gauge is acceptable, since 35% of the variance is small
the gauge is unacceptable for charting: over the 30% threshold, and its ndc is 3
the control limits should simply be widened
the process is out of control
quiz.solution: Above 30% is not acceptable for process control. The binding consequence is resolution: \( \mathrm{ndc}=\lfloor1.41\times11.05/4.11\rfloor=3 \), where five is the usual minimum for a variables chart, so the chart is largely plotting the instrument. Widening the limits is what the inflated data already did, and it is the problem rather than the fix.

quiz.q: With GRR 4.11 and TV 11.79 µm, the gauge's share of the variance is
quiz.solution: \( 4.11^2/11.79^2=16.90/138.92=12.2\% \). The 34.9% is the ratio of standard deviations, and 6.7% is how much the observed \( \sigma \) is inflated. Because the terms combine in quadrature, a \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) that sounds alarming distorts a capability index only modestly — here \( C_p \) reads 1.41 instead of 1.51.

quiz.q: The number of distinct categories is \( \lfloor\sqrt2\,\mathrm{PV}/\mathrm{GRR}\rfloor \). Its practical significance is that
choices: below 5 a variables control chart is largely plotting the gauge
it sets the sample size for the study
it must exceed the number of operators
quiz.solution: ndc counts the non-overlapping intervals of gauge uncertainty that fit inside the part spread — how many genuinely different values the gauge can tell apart. Five is the usual minimum for a variables chart; at 3 the gauge is closer to an attribute device. It complements \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) rather than replacing it, and it is usually the more damning of the two.

quiz.q: A study finds \( \sigma_{\text{EV}}=3.19 \) and \( \sigma_{\text{AV}}=2.59\ \mu\mathrm{m} \). The most effective response is to
choices: improve the gauge, fixture or method, since 60% of the variance is repeatability
increase the number of parts in the study
quiz.solution: \( 10.17 \) against \( 6.73 \) of variance: the equipment and method carry the larger share, so training addresses the smaller one. Averaging three readings, which divides the repeatability variance by three, takes \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) from 34.9% to 27.7% and ndc from 3 to 4 — bought with time rather than capital. Had AV dominated, averaging would have bought almost nothing.

quiz.q: A gauge with \( \mathrm{GRR}=4.11\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) is used to accept parts against a 100 µm tolerance, with a guard band giving 95% one-sided confidence. The band consumes
quiz.solution: \( 1.645\times4.11=6.76\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) at each end, so 13.5 µm of 100. With a 1.0 µm gauge the same confidence costs 3.3%. Stating the gauge's cost as lost tolerance is usually more persuasive than \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \), because tolerance is the thing a shop is short of.

quiz.q: An instrument displaying to 5 µm contributes a standard deviation of about
quiz.solution: Rounding to a resolution \( q \) contributes a variance \( q^2/12 \), so \( 5/\sqrt{12}=1.44\ \mu\mathrm{m} \) — a fifth of the repeatability in the worked study, from the display alone. At 1 µm it is 0.29 µm and negligible. Being unbiased does not make it free; it is a variance, not an offset.

quiz.q: A gauge study is run on ten parts hand-picked from the middle of the process distribution. The reported \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) will be
choices: unaffected, since GRR does not depend on the parts
too high, because PV has been artificially shrunk
too low, because the parts are more similar
quiz.solution: \( \%\mathrm{GRR} \) compares the gauge with the part variation, so narrowing the parts inflates the ratio and condemns an adequate gauge. The study's parts must span the real process range. The mirror error — deliberately including extreme parts — flatters the gauge for the same reason.

10.kuwait:
Applied case — the charts that were plotting the instrument. A machining cell put \( \bar X \)–\( R \) charts on a bore diameter and ran them for a year. The charts were noisy, signalled often, and every investigation ended without a finding; operators came to treat the signals as background and stopped recording them.

A gauge study run afterwards explained the year. With \( \bar R=5.4 \), \( R_o=4.5 \) and \( R_p=34\ \mu\mathrm{m} \), the measuring system's own standard deviation was 4.11 µm against a part variation of 11.05, giving \( \%\mathrm{GRR}=34.9\% \) and \( \mathrm{ndc}=3 \) — three distinguishable categories across the whole process range. The within-subgroup ranges the limits were computed from were largely the gauge, so the limits were too wide to catch real shifts and the point-to-point scatter that looked like an unstable process was the instrument. Sixty per cent of the gauge's variance was repeatability, so the cure was the fixture and the method rather than the operators who had been repeatedly asked to be more careful.

Two practices follow. Run the study before the charts, not after: everything computed from measured data inherits the measuring system's variance, so a study run afterwards can only tell you which of the past year's conclusions to discard. And when a chart signals repeatedly with no assignable cause ever found, treat the measuring system as a suspect equal to the process — a year of unexplained signals is itself evidence, and it costs one study to check.

  • Repeatability is one operator, one part, one gauge, repeated; reproducibility is between operators — usually the work instruction rather than the people.

  • The worked study gives EV 3.19, AV 2.59, GRR 4.11, PV 11.05 and TV 11.79 µm.
  • Two verdicts, two questions: \( \%\mathrm{GRR}=34.9\% \) against the process (unacceptable for charting) and 24.7% against a 100 µm tolerance (marginal for accept/reject).
  • Quadrature is forgiving: 34.9% of \( \sigma \) is only 12.2% of the variance, inflates \( \sigma \) by 6.7% and costs 6.3% of \( C_p \).
  • Resolution is what it destroys: \( \mathrm{ndc}=3 \) against a usual minimum of 5, and an \( \bar X \) chart 22% slower to catch a \( 1\sigma \) shift (ARL 5.47 against 4.50).

  • Resolution contributes \( q^2/12 \): a 5 µm display adds 1.44 µm, a 1 µm display 0.29.

11.lecture:
§1 · Say it, do it, prove it

A quality management system looks, from outside, like a great deal of paper. Reduced to its logic it is three obligations, and every clause of a standard such as ISO 9001 exists to serve one of them: say what you intend to do, do it, and prove that you did. Document control, competence, management review and internal audit are the machinery; those three are the content.

Map that onto the calibration programme this course has been building and it stops being abstract. Say is a written procedure naming which instruments are controlled, the standard each is calibrated against, the interval, the acceptance criterion, who is competent to do it, and — the clause most often missing — what happens when an instrument is found out of tolerance. Do is instruments uniquely identified and labelled with a due date, calibrated by the stated method against traceable standards, with the traceability chain of Lesson 1 unbroken. Prove is the retained evidence: certificates carrying uncertainties, a record of every event, the uncertainty budgets of Lesson 3, the out-of-tolerance investigations, and the recall decisions that followed them.

The three failure modes are worth naming because each is common and each looks different in an audit. Say without do is paperwork — a procedure nobody follows, which is worse than no procedure because it is a documented commitment being breached. Do without say is craft: it may be excellent, it is not repeatable when the person leaves, and it cannot be defended to a customer. Do without prove is the one that catches good shops, because the work really was done and there is no evidence of it. In an audit, unprovable and undone are the same finding.

§2 · Nonconformance, and the difference CAPA depends on

A nonconformance is any failure to meet a requirement — a part outside its tolerance, a procedure not followed, an instrument past its due date. The record of one has a fixed shape: what was found, how much, where and by whom, what was done to contain it, and how it was disposed of. Disposition is a decision among use-as-is, rework, repair, regrade and scrap, and it is an engineering judgement that belongs to someone with the authority to make it, not to whoever found the problem.

Key distinction — the three actions

Correction fixes the affected product. Corrective action removes the cause so it does not recur. Preventive action acts on a cause that has not produced a failure yet.

Scrapping the batch is a correction. Re-cutting the fixture location that let the batch happen is a corrective action. They are routinely confused, and a system that only ever performs corrections will keep meeting the same nonconformance and closing it every time.

Both words are overloaded, and this course has already used them in other senses. A correction in Lesson 3 was the value added to a reading to remove a known bias; a disposition in Lesson 5 was how a gauge tolerance is placed inside a work tolerance. Neither has anything to do with the meanings here, and reading a nonconformance record with the metrology sense in mind is a genuine source of confusion.

Two disciplines make the difference real. The first is containment: the question is never only what is wrong with this part but what else is affected — which other batches, which other characteristics, what is already at the customer. The second is the effectiveness check: after a corrective action, evidence that the recurrence rate actually fell. A corrective action closed without one is a promise rather than an action, and it is the single most common weakness a third-party auditor finds.

The bridge to the rest of this course is that an instrument found out of tolerance at calibration is a nonconformance, and its containment scope is set by something already chosen: the calibration interval. Everything measured since the last good calibration is suspect, because nothing distinguishes readings taken before the drift from readings taken after it.

§3 · What a calibration interval is really buying

That last observation turns the interval from an administrative setting into an arithmetic one.

Key relations — exposure and the optimum interval

\[ N_{\text{suspect}}\approx r\,\frac{T}{2},\qquad K(T)=\frac{C_c}{T}+\frac{r\lambda T}{2}C_p,\qquad T^{*}=\sqrt{\frac{2C_c}{r\lambda C_p}} \]

\( r \) is the production rate, \( T \) the interval, \( \lambda \) the rate at which instruments drift out of tolerance, \( C_c \) the cost of one calibration and \( C_p \) the cost of dealing with one suspect part. If the drift can have occurred at any time in the interval, the expected exposure is half of it.

Take a line measuring 400 parts a day over 250 working days — 100,000 a year. On a twelve-month interval, an instrument found out of tolerance implicates on average six months of production: 50,000 parts, every one of which has to be re-inspected, justified, or accepted on an engineering rationale. On a three-month interval the same finding implicates 12,500. Nothing about the instrument changed; the exposure was set by a decision made a year earlier.

Neither extreme is right, because calibrating costs money too. Differentiating \( K(T) \) and setting the derivative to zero — the standard minimisation from Engineering Mathematics I — gives \( T^{*} \). With \( C_c=120 \), \( r=100{,}000 \), \( \lambda=0.15 \) per year and \( C_p=0.05 \), the optimum is 0.566 years, or 6.8 months, at an annual cost of 424. At that interval the two cost terms are each 212: at the optimum the cost of calibrating equals the cost of the exposure, which is a quick way to test an existing interval without redoing the calculus.

The shape of the curve matters as much as its minimum. Twelve months costs 495, 17% more; three months costs 574, 35% more. Over-calibrating is the more expensive error here, which is not the intuition most shops have, and the asymmetry comes from the \( C_c/T \) term rising without bound as the interval shrinks. Two qualifications keep this honest: \( \lambda \) has to come from the instrument's own drift history rather than from a table, and an instrument whose out-of-tolerance would implicate a safety characteristic is not on this curve at all, because \( C_p \) is not a re-inspection cost in that case.

§4 · Audits, maintenance records, and what "no findings" is worth

Audits come in three flavours — internal, done to yourself; second-party, done by a customer; third-party, done by a certification body — and all three work the same way. The auditor picks an endpoint and traces it backwards until the chain either closes or does not: a certificate on a wall back to the standard it was measured against, a part in a box back to the inspection record and the instrument that produced it, a control chart back to the gauge study that justified it.

Maintenance records enter that chain in three places, and shops are regularly surprised by all three. Equipment that produces or verifies product is subject to control, so a machine whose scheduled maintenance lapsed is direct evidence against the claim that the process was in control. Calibration is maintenance of the measuring system, so the two record sets have to agree about the same instrument's history — a repair in one that does not appear in the other is a finding on both. And after a nonconformance the maintenance log is where a root cause is confirmed or refuted: a spindle bearing replaced the same week the ranges on a chart widened is the strongest evidence anyone will get. The finding that catches good shops is a capability study performed before a major overhaul and never repeated after it: the evidence describes a machine that no longer exists.

Finally, what an audit result actually means, because an audit is a sample and everything this course knows about samples applies to it.

Key relations — the audit as a sample

\[ P(\text{find at least one})=1-(1-p)^{n},\qquad p_{95\%}\le 1-0.05^{1/n}\approx\frac{3}{n} \]

The first sizes an audit: to be 95% confident of finding a nonconformity present in 5% of records, \( n=\ln0.05/\ln0.95=58.4 \), so 59 records. The second reads a clean one: finding nothing in \( n \) records bounds the nonconformity rate at roughly \( 3/n \), not at zero.

Thirty records with no findings supports the statement "the nonconformity rate is below about 9.5%" and supports nothing stronger. Twenty records supports 13.9%. Neither is "the system conforms", and an internal audit programme that samples twenty records a quarter and reports no findings has demonstrated very little at considerable expense. The remedy is the same one Lesson 9 reached: sample size buys discrimination, so audit deeply in the areas where a failure would be expensive and accept that the shallow areas are being spot-checked rather than verified.

Which is the honest closing position for the whole course. A measurement is a claim about a part; a quality system is what makes that claim mean something six months later, to someone who was not there, about a part they cannot re-measure. The instrument, the uncertainty budget, the chart, the capability study and the audit trail are one apparatus, and the weakest of them sets what the rest is worth.

quiz.q:
Price a calibration interval

Problem. A line measures 100,000 parts a year with one instrument. A calibration event costs 120, instruments drift out of tolerance at \( \lambda=0.15 \) per year, and each part implicated by an out-of-tolerance finding costs 0.05 to re-inspect. Write the annual cost as a function of the interval \( T \) in years, find the optimum interval in years, months and weeks, and compare the annual cost there with the cost at twelve months and at three months.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) Calibrations occur \( 1/T \) times a year, costing \( C_c/T \). If the drift can start at any time in the interval, the expected exposure is \( T/2 \), so the expected parts implicated per year are \( r\lambda T/2 \), each costing \( C_p \). Hence \( K(T)=\dfrac{C_c}{T}+\dfrac{r\lambda T}{2}C_p \).

(2) \( \dfrac{dK}{dT}=-\dfrac{C_c}{T^2}+\dfrac{r\lambda C_p}{2}=0 \), so \( T^{*}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2C_c}{r\lambda C_p}} \). The second derivative \( 2C_c/T^3 \) is positive, so it is a minimum.

(3) \( T^{*}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(120)}{100000(0.15)(0.05)}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{240}{750}}=\sqrt{0.32} =0.566\ \mathrm{yr} \), that is 6.79 months or 29.4 weeks.

(4) \( K(T^{*})=120/0.566+100000(0.15)(0.566)(0.05)/2=212.13+212.13=424.26 \).

(5) \( K(1)=120+375=495 \), which is \( 495/424.26-1=16.7\% \) more.

(6) \( K(0.25)=480+93.75=573.75 \), which is 35.2% more.

Answer: \( T^{*}=0.566 \) yr = 6.79 months = 29.4 weeks, at an annual cost of 424.26; twelve months costs 495 (17% more) and three months 574 (35% more). Sanity check: at the optimum the two cost terms are each 212.13 — exactly equal, which is a general property of this cost shape and the fastest way to audit an existing interval without redoing the calculus. Note the asymmetry: over-calibrating costs more than under-calibrating here, because \( C_c/T \) grows without bound as \( T\to0 \) while the exposure term only grows linearly. Note finally what the model assumes — \( \lambda \) from the instrument's own drift history, and \( C_p \) a re-inspection cost. If the characteristic is safety-related, \( C_p \) is not a re-inspection cost and the instrument does not belong on this curve.

quiz.q:
An out-of-tolerance finding, and what it implicates

Problem. A bore gauge on a line producing 400 parts a day, 250 days a year, is found at its annual calibration to read 0.0001 in high. Express the error in micrometres. Assuming the drift could have begun at any time since the last good calibration, find the expected number of parts implicated on a twelve-month interval, a 6.79-month interval and a three-month interval. State what the quality system must record, and name the three actions the finding calls for.
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) \( 0.0001\ \mathrm{in}\times25.4\ \mathrm{mm/in}=0.00254\ \mathrm{mm}=2.54\ \mu\mathrm{m} \).

(2) The line makes \( 400\times250=100{,}000 \) parts a year. Nothing distinguishes readings taken before the drift from readings taken after it, so everything since the last good calibration is suspect, and the expected exposure is half the interval.

(3) Twelve months: \( 100{,}000\times\tfrac{1}{2}=50{,}000 \) parts.

(4) 6.79 months: \( 100{,}000\times\tfrac{0.566}{2}=28{,}300 \) parts.

(5) Three months: \( 100{,}000\times\tfrac{0.25}{2}=12{,}500 \) parts.

(6) The record must carry the finding and its magnitude, the containment scope and how it was determined, the disposition of the affected population, the root cause, and an effectiveness check.

(7) The three actions: correction — adjust or replace the gauge and deal with the implicated parts; corrective action — remove whatever let the drift go undetected, which here is the interval itself or the absence of an intermediate check; preventive action — review other instruments on the same duty cycle before they do the same thing.

Answer: 2.54 µm; 50,000 parts implicated at twelve months, 28,300 at 6.79 and 12,500 at three; the containment scope is set by the interval, and the finding calls for a correction, a corrective action and a preventive action. Sanity check: the instrument's behaviour was identical in all three cases — only a decision made a year earlier changed the size of the problem, which is exactly why the interval is an engineering choice rather than an administrative one. Note the value of an intermediate check: verifying the gauge against a reference block weekly would cap the exposure at a week's production regardless of the calibration interval, which is usually far cheaper than shortening the interval itself.

quiz.q:
What a clean audit is worth

Problem. An internal audit samples records at random from a large population in which a fraction \( p \) are nonconforming. Find the sample size needed for a 95% chance of finding at least one nonconformity when \( p=0.05 \). Then find the probability of finding at least one from a sample of 30, and the 95% upper bound on \( p \) implied by finding none in 20 and in 30 records. Compare the exact bound with the "rule of three".
quiz.solution:
Solution. (1) The chance of missing every nonconformity is \( (1-p)^n \), so \( P(\text{at least one})=1-(1-p)^n \). Setting this to 0.95 gives \( (0.95)^n=0.05 \), so \( n=\ln0.05/\ln0.95=58.4 \) → 59 records.

(2) From 30 records: \( 1-0.95^{30}=1-0.2146=0.785 \). A one-in-five chance of missing a nonconformity running at 5%.

(3) Finding none in \( n \) records is consistent with any \( p \) for which \( (1-p)^n\ge0.05 \), so the 95% upper bound is \( p\le1-0.05^{1/n} \).

(4) \( n=20 \): \( 1-0.05^{1/20}=1-0.8609=13.9\% \). \( n=30 \): \( 1-0.05^{1/30}=1-0.9050=9.50\% \).

(5) The rule of three gives \( 3/20=15\% \) and \( 3/30=10\% \) — within a point of the exact values, and it needs no calculator.

Answer: 59 records for 95% confidence at \( p=0.05 \); 0.785 from a sample of 30; a clean audit of 20 bounds \( p \) at 13.9% and of 30 at 9.5%, against 15% and 10% from the rule of three. Sanity check: "no findings" from twenty records supports the claim that nonconformity is below about 14%, which is a much weaker statement than the phrase suggests and is the honest way to report it. The arithmetic is the same as Lesson 9's: a sample bounds a rate and never demonstrates zero. The practical consequence is to audit deeply where a failure would be expensive and to say plainly that the rest was spot-checked rather than verified.

quiz.q: A shop performs a calibration correctly but retains no record of it. In an audit this is
choices: acceptable, since the work was actually done
indistinguishable from not having done it
a nonconformance against the calibrating laboratory
quiz.solution: Prove is one of the three obligations, not an afterthought to the other two. An auditor can only assess evidence, so unprovable and undone produce the same finding. This is the failure mode that catches competent shops, because the work genuinely was done and there is nothing to show for it.

quiz.q: A batch is scrapped after a fixture was found mislocated. Scrapping the batch is
quiz.solution: It fixes the affected product, which is a correction. The corrective action is whatever stops the fixture being mislocated again — a location feature, a check in the setup sheet. A system that only performs corrections meets the same nonconformance repeatedly and closes it every time.

quiz.q: A corrective action is closed without an effectiveness check. The consequence is that
choices: nothing, if the root cause was correctly identified
there is no evidence the recurrence rate actually fell, so the action is a promise rather than a result
the nonconformance record must be reopened automatically
the auditor cannot raise a finding
quiz.solution: The check is what converts an intended fix into a demonstrated one, and its absence is among the commonest third-party findings. Identifying a plausible root cause is not the same as showing the action removed it — the failure may recur for a reason nobody listed.

quiz.q: An instrument is found out of tolerance at its annual calibration. The population of suspect parts is
choices: only the parts measured that day
everything measured since the last good calibration
nothing, provided the instrument is adjusted
quiz.solution: Nothing in the readings distinguishes those taken before the drift from those taken after it, so the containment scope runs back to the last calibration that passed. On a line making 100,000 parts a year and an annual interval, that is 50,000 parts on average — a number fixed by a decision made a year earlier, not by the instrument.

quiz.q: With \( K(T)=C_c/T+r\lambda TC_p/2 \), at the optimum interval
choices: the two cost terms are equal
quiz.solution: Setting \( dK/dT=0 \) gives \( C_c/T^2=r\lambda C_p/2 \), and multiplying by \( T \) shows \( C_c/T=r\lambda TC_p/2 \). Here each is 212.13 against a total of 424.26. It is the quickest audit of an existing interval: if one term dominates, the interval is wrong in the direction of the larger term.

quiz.q: An internal audit samples 30 records and finds no nonconformities. The strongest honest conclusion is
choices: the nonconformity rate is below about 9.5% with 95% confidence
the sample was too small to conclude anything at all
quiz.solution: \( 1-0.05^{1/30}=9.5\% \), close to the rule of three's \( 3/30=10\% \). A sample bounds a rate and never demonstrates zero — the same arithmetic as an acceptance sampling plan. Reporting "no findings" without the bound overstates what was demonstrated, and 30 records is not nothing, it is simply a weak bound.

quiz.q: To be 95% confident of finding a nonconformity present in 5% of records, an audit must sample about
quiz.solution: \( (0.95)^n=0.05 \) gives \( n=\ln0.05/\ln0.95=58.4 \), so 59. Most internal audits sample far fewer, which is a legitimate choice provided the report says what was actually demonstrated. Sample size buys discrimination in an audit exactly as it does in an acceptance plan.

quiz.q: A machine's capability study was performed before a major overhaul and never repeated. In an audit this is a finding because
choices: capability studies expire after twelve months by rule
the evidence describes a machine that no longer exists
the study should have used more parts
quiz.solution: An overhaul changes the equipment the evidence was about, so the study no longer supports any claim regarding the current machine. This is where maintenance records enter the audit trail: they are what reveals that the evidence and the equipment have diverged, and they are also where a root cause is confirmed after a nonconformance.

11.kuwait:
Applied case — the finding that arrived a year late. A bore gauge on a line running 400 parts a day was calibrated annually. At one calibration it was found reading 2.54 µm high. The instrument was adjusted, the certificate was filed, and production continued. Eleven months later a customer returned a batch of undersized bores, and the investigation could not establish when the drift had begun.

The system had performed the correction and neither of the other two actions. The containment question — what else is affected — was never asked, and its answer was fixed by the interval: with 100,000 parts a year and nothing to distinguish readings before the drift from readings after it, the expected suspect population was 50,000 parts. Nor was there a corrective action, because the cause of the late detection was the interval itself and the absence of any intermediate check, and adjusting the gauge addressed neither. The certificate on file recorded that the instrument had been adjusted and proved nothing about the parts, which is the "prove" obligation failing while looking as though it had been met.

Two practices follow. Treat an out-of-tolerance finding as a nonconformance with a containment scope, not as a maintenance event: the first question is which parts, and the answer is already determined by the interval, so it can be worked out before the finding ever occurs. And where the exposure is large, buy detection rather than frequency — a weekly check against a reference block caps the suspect population at a week's production for a fraction of the cost of shortening the calibration interval, and it turns an unanswerable question into a bounded one.
11.recap:
• A quality system reduces to three obligations — say it, do it, prove it — and every clause of a standard serves one of them.
  • Mapped onto calibration: the written procedure and its out-of-tolerance clause; identified instruments calibrated against traceable standards; and retained certificates, budgets, investigations and recall decisions.
  • Say without do is paperwork, do without say is craft, and do without prove is indistinguishable from undone in an audit.
  • Correction fixes the product, corrective action removes the cause, preventive action acts on a cause not yet realised. A system that only corrects meets the same nonconformance forever.
  • Containment and the effectiveness check are what make a corrective action real; without the second it is a promise.
  • An out-of-tolerance instrument is a nonconformance whose containment scope was fixed by the calibration interval: \( N\approx rT/2 \), so 50,000 parts at 100,000/year on a twelve-month interval and 12,500 on a three-month one.
  • \( K(T)=C_c/T+r\lambda TC_p/2 \) minimises at \( T^{*}=\sqrt{2C_c/(r\lambda C_p)}=6.8 \) months here, costing 424 a year.
  • At the optimum the two cost terms are equal (212 each) — the fastest test of an existing interval. Twelve months costs 17% more, three months 35% more.
  • Maintenance records enter the audit trail three ways: equipment control, agreement with the calibration history, and root-cause confirmation — and a capability study never repeated after an overhaul describes a machine that no longer exists.
  • An audit is a sample: 59 records for 95% confidence of catching a 5% nonconformity, and finding nothing in 30 bounds the rate at 9.5%, close to the rule of three's \( 3/n \). "No findings" is a bound, never a zero.
